Mr. Chairman, this question of freight rates is certainly one of the matters in which the people of Canada are most interested at the present time. After a careful study of this important matter, which carries with it the possibility of unpredictable repercussions upon the economic life of our nation, one would reach the conclusion that above the dollars and cents aspect a great principle is involved which cannot be overlooked by those of us who wish to maintain our present way of life.
There are at least two historic conceptions of how the subordination of the individual or of private enterprise to the common good is to be effected and maintained. One is that the state is the supreme entity and the people its instruments, in complete submission to its dictates and purposes. The other is that the people are supreme, that the state is the creation of their will and the instrument of their purpose to live together for the common good. A few years ago we ended the second world war fought to maintain this latter type of state and government. Our soldiers protected it from the enemies who would have destroyed it by force from without. Our task today is to protect it from

Supply-Transport
shipping his goods five hundred miles have his rates increased by the same number of dollars and cents as would the man shipping his goods a thousand miles? That is the result of applying a maximum increase.
Railway rates should be at such a level that there is, after payment of expenses, an adequate return on the money invested in railway enterprises. Unless we are going to change our way of life, as I said a moment ago, this view must be true, whether the money invested is government money, as in the Canadian National Railways, or privately invested money, as in the Canadian Pacific Railway.
This committee knows that the Canadian National Railways has been able to pay its operating expenses but has not been able to pay its fixed charges, or provide a return on the investment in the railway property. In 1948 the Canadian Pacific Railway had a return of only 1.80 per cent on its investment in railway property; that is, the net investment after full deduction for depreciation. In 1949 the return on the net railway property investment of Canadian Pacific Railway was only 1.97 per cent. These figures can be secured from the evidence given by the Canadian Pacific Railway to the royal commission on transportation. Therefore, investors in the Canadian Pacific Railway have no guarantee that they will secure a return on their investment; but in prosperous times lor the railway to be able to earn only less than 2 per cent on its net rail property investment is obviously inadequate treatment of private investors.
Certainly no one will allege that Canadian railways are not efficiently managed. And no one will deny that the employees of such railways are good citizens, striving to do a good job and to give Canada outstanding service. I need merely point to the tremendous and efficient job performed by railway employees and railway management during the last war to prove that railway employees and management are industrious, resourceful and efficient.
The efficiency of Canadian railways can still be improved by the railways securing new types of locomotives, such as diesels and other modern machines, and rearranging their plants, such as their yard's, so that traffic can be handled more cheaply and more speedily. To carry out these improvements, railways require money. The only place, for example, the Canadian Pacific Railway as a private enterprise can secure that money is from private investors. For private investors to lend their money to the Canadian Pacific Railway, such investors must have a fair chance of a reasonable return on the money they lend.

In conclusion, may I quote an excerpt from the evidence of the chairman of the Canadian Pacific Railway, Mr. George A. Walker, before the royal commission on transportation on December 12, 1949, when he stated:
It has been the consistent policy of successive governments of our country and was recently reaffirmed by the Prime Minister of Canada that "the best way to maintain a high level of employment and to ensure prosperity is to provide the widest possible scope for private enterprise." No major political party in this country has ever adopted a contrary attitude.
As the first great enterprise in Canada, one which was an essential link in confederation itself and which is still the greatest single enterprise in this country, the Canadian Pacific may justly claim the benefit and protection of such a government policy in as full measure as, but no more than, industry generally throughout Canada.
Finally I would like to say this. Surely this committee will agree that it is not equipped to deal with freight rate details. Most of us will come to the conclusion that the board of transport commissioners should be left to handle this problem on- the evidence presented, and bring to bear their wide experience in arriving at a fair a-nd just conclusion for the common good of the whole Canadian community. Unless we are prepared to leave the matter to the board of transport commissioners we must, admittedly ill equipped, deal with it ourselves. Surely no one who has given any serious thought to the question would suggest that as a solution.
Canadian- railways must be allowed to live and to live dynamically. Let us support the experienced and qualified judgment of the board. Let us not hamper the railways from living by attempting to place our inexperienced judgment above that of the board of transport commissioners, to which parliament has given the task of seeing that the railways and the public are fairly and justly treated.
I sincerely hope that the house will agree that, through the board of transport commissioners, private enterprise, which is seeking no favours or special privileges but only fair and just treatment in this matter, will be fostered.

Mr. Chairman, the question of freight rates as applied to western Canada divides itself into two distinct compartments. In one compartment are the rates set by the Crowsnest agreement, which cannot be interfered with, and in the other compartment are the rates that vary.
In today's discussion we have heard the rates for Canada generally discussed, and very little has been said about the Crowsnest pass agreement. I think perhaps it might be wise at this time to say a few words in explanation to those who do not know the

reason for its existence and how it came about. In the early part of the settlement of western Canada we found ourselves with a completed trans-Canada railroad. In the prairie provinces there were about 300,000 people. They were discontented. There were high freight rates, and settlement was at a standstill. Eastern Canada itself had only about five million people.
It was decided that to develop the country a vigorous program of immigration must be introduced, that the people of eastern Canada must depend upon western Canada to purchase everything that they required to settle that country. The natural market for the prairie country lies to the south. The great lakes region prevented our coming east. The Rocky mountains prevented our going west; trade was naturally with the people to the south.
The Canadian Pacific Railway wanted to overcome this, and therefore built a line from Lethbridge to Nelson, so that it would get in and shut off the traffic which was going from southwestern Alberta and southern British Columbia into the United States. It had been promised then that immigration would be strongly supported. This road was built, and for that the Canadian government gave to the C.P.R. a subsidy of $3,404,000 and from British Columbia it received a land grant of 3,620,000 acres with the mineral rights, and 60 square miles of coal land. They obtained a monopoly on the transportation to southern Alberta, and therefore were in a most favourable position to control trade there.
We know what has resulted from this. The great Trail smelters have developed into one of the greatest sources of income for the C.P.R. today. For this what did the railway give? It gave the Crowsnest pass agreement which was an undertaking that it would reduce the rates on grain to the extent of three cents per hundred pounds shipped from prairie points to the lakes. It also agreed to bring settlers effects, machinery and other essential goods for settlement from eastern Canada at a favoured rate amounting to a reduction of from 10 to 33^ per cent. These rates were set up and were to constitute the maximum for all time. The C.P.R. set the rate that it would give.
Owing to competition from the Canadian National Railways, which came into Manitoba, an agreement was made whereby the maximum rate was not changed until 1918. In 1918 a Tory or union government at Ottawa did away with the Crowsnest pass agreement. This may be surprising to some Conservative members when they learn about it. But
Supply-Transport
thanks to an alert senator, Senator Watson, the Senate did not approve of the -bill with the result that the rates were only suspended for three years. They rose above the maximum set by the Crowsnest pass agreement; but in 1922 a Liberal government again restored the rates on wheat and flour moving from the prairie provinces to Fort William. The rates on commodities moving west were restored in 1924.
Then arose a dispute as to the application of the agreement. The railways claimed that the rates applied only to points in existence when the act was passed, and that from any other points they could charge full rates. The submission to the royal commission on transportation by the pools in January of this year contains the following:
Upon reinstatement of the Crowsnest pass rates in their entirety, July 7, 1924, the C.P.R. for the first time took the position that the agreement only applied to shipping points which were in existence in 1897. It accordingly ignored the maximum set by the agreement in so far as all other points were concerned. The discrimination and confusion thus created brought about appeals to the board of railway commissioners, and the government alike. The board held that the provisions of the agreement had been overridden by the Railway Act and it, therefore, restored the rates in existence prior to July 7, 1924, which on westbound freight were at a level higher than the maximum set by the agreement.
The board's decision was reversed by the Supreme Court of Canada, which held that the Crowsnest agreement was binding upon the railroad and the railway commissioners, but only applied to shipping points in existence in 1897.
The Parliament of Canada in 1925 intervened by relieving the railway company of its obligations under the agreement with regard to all commodities shipped from eastern Canada to the west. Thereby it removed the ceiling set by the agreement on all such commodities. At the same time, parliament not only refused to relieve the railway company of its obligations with regard to grain and flour rates, but enacted that they should apply to all shipping points, irrespective of whether or not they were in existence in 1897.
It is as a result of this Crowsnest pass agreement that the Maritime Freight Rates Act was passed, giving a 20 per cent reduction in freight rates to the maritimes. It was also responsible for the removal of the mountain differential, which was first reduced and then completely abolished by a Liberal government.
The Winnipeg Free Press of November 3, 1924, reports Mr. Mackenzie King as having said: "The east is protected by waterways, the Pacific by the Panama canal and the west by parliament." It is just that protection from monopoly that we in the west are asking for today. We are forced to sell on the open market; we are forced to export principally through eastern Canada and British Columbia. I believe the Hudson Bay route has not been given a fair trial, and with modern radar

Supply-Transport
equipment and a modern icebreaker I am confident that port could be kept open longer than it is now.
I discussed this matter with the wheat pool and asked them why they were not using the port to a greater extent. They said they could not ship grain from Canada until the consignment had been sold in England. I asked them what they did in winter in respect of consignments going abroad, and whether they could not build in England or Scotland a terminal elevator to which they could ship during the summer months and in which they could hold the wheat for delivery, just as they ship to Portland or Halifax or Saint John for winter delivery now. That would save us a considerable amount in freight rates, and! we have to look for every avenue of saving on freight rates if we are going to compete in the markets of Europe. Eastern Canada has profited greatly from this handling of grain. We do not complain about this, but what is our position when we come to buy? Our natural market lies to the south in Minneapolis and St. Paul and in the large implement houses in the midwest. Freights from there are much lower and we could obtain our farm implements at much lower prices. But, no. Although we are forced to sell on the open market, we must buy in a closed market and pay for the high protection that is necessary to develop industries in Canada as well as the long freight haul from eastern to western Canada. We did not complain about this until the rates became discriminatory, hut the recent rate increases have resulted in a difference of 15 per cent between the eastern and western rates. The real issue here is that of discrimination, not just freight rates.
I should like to refer to a suggestion made by Mr. Tucker, the leader of the opposition in Saskatchewan. He suggests that payment be made to the railroads from the federal treasury, by all the people of Canada, of an amount sufficient to take care of the cost of bridging the gap between the different settled areas of Canada, and then when that is done equalized freight rates should be established right across the country. Of course, close account would have to be kept of the railway operations and accounting systems.
We in western Canada feel that we have some protection in the Crowsnest pass agreement. We paid for it and it never should be abrogated. We almost lost it when the union government was in power, but Senator Watson picked it up in the Senate; otherwise we would not have any agreement today. When I hear someone talking about the reform of the Senate I am inclined to think that at that time it was probably a little 
brighter than the House of Commons. All the railway acts, all royal commissions, the board of railway commissioners now the board of transport commissioners, were brought into being or set up by Liberal governments. I fail to see any basis for the opposition amendment. As one representing a western constituency I call upon the government to exercise its authority and see that injustices are not permitted.
Before closing I should like to comment upon a few of the things said by a most inconsistent gentleman, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. I am sorry he is not in his seat, but I am sure the hon. member for Cape Breton South will report what I am saying to him. Normally the hon. gentleman advocates state control, but this morning he was advocating keen competition among the railways. He protests that the freight rate increases are too great and should not be granted. I should like to quote an editorial that appeared in the Ottawa Journal of February 1, 1950, as follows:
Payment by somebody else
Three western grain organizations appeared before the royal commission on transportation this week to attack railway wage scales. They said the railways' payrolls were too heavy, that rail wages and salaries should be re-examined before attempt was made to increase rates on grain.
Too bad these western grain organizations (Manitoba pool elevators, Saskatchewan co-operative producers and the Alberta wheat pool) did not think of that before. For had they thought of it a year or so ago, when the railways, faced with higher wage demands, were saying that higher wages must mean higher freight rates, their thought might have meant something.
As it was, the railways were left to fight their own battle. The western grain organizations were silent. The provinces were silent. The politicians were silent.
As a consequence, this happened:	That when a
conciliation board decided the railway employees should get so much and the railway employees insisted on more, the dominion government, not hearing any protests from the western grain organizations nor from the provinces nor from anybody else, stepped in and said the employees must have more.
The railways agreed; they had no alternative. As Mr. Justice Rand put it in the supreme court some weeks ago, they (the railways) "paid what they had to pay." And when they paid, and the stage was necessarily set for higher freight rates (for how else were the railways to get the money to pay the new wage costs?) not a word came from the west. The government wasn't told that by compelling the railways to pay higher wages (higher even than a conciliation board held to be fair) it was incurring the danger of higher grain rates. If the thing was thought about at all, it apparently was thought of with the idea-so common these days-that payment would be by somebody else.
It will be remembered that this morning the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar protested against any increase in rail rates. However, the railways have shown distinctly that

the increases in freight rates that were given have all been taken up by the payment of higher wages to the brotherhood of railway workers. Is the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar opposed to those increases in wages to the brotherhood of railway workers?
That is the point.

I am sorry the hon. member is not here to answer that question. Is that what he was supporting when he spoke in favour of the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition? He is rather inconsistent on that point. I should like to comment on the attitude taken this morning by the leader of the opposition, who has a friendly habit of giving the supporters of the government a lecture on their responsibilities as members and on the duty they owe to their constituents. I have no doubt that he finds these lectures useful and perhaps necessary as far as his own followers are concerned, but I assure him that we new members are fully aware of our responsibilities and we are accustomed to fulfilling our duties.
The leader of the opposition asks us to support his amendment and he says that this government has done nothing. Surely he realizes that every freight rate act was brought in by a Liberal government? Surely he realizes that if it had not been for a Liberal government we would have lost our Crowsnest pass rates? The appointment of royal commissions and everything else has been the work of Liberal governments. I simply wanted to state my reasons why I could not support the amendment, and I hope I have stated them clearly so that my friends may understand.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Regina City with regard to the freight rates situation and his reply to the leader of the opposition; but he did not discuss the point that this increase will accentuate the discrimination. Nothing has been said by any previous speaker supporting the government as to the removal of discrimination in the freight rate structure. As I listened to the minister speak I began to realize that there was no hope for western Canada and the maritime provinces at all for relief against the increase in discrimination against these areas brought about by continuing horizontal increases in railway freight rates. When the hon. member for Regina City dealt with this question and went back into the history of the Crowsnest rates instead of dealing with the resolution now before the house, I could only conclude that no member from the province of Saskatchewan or the other western provinces can
Supply-Transport
deny the grave injustice that is being intensified by reason of allowing this further increase in railway rates. It is in no way a question whether the railways should be able to finance and return a profit. All of us believe that there must necessarily be an increase in railway rates in order to meet increased costs of operation, wages and the like, provided that the companies are able to establish the necessity for such increases.
What we from the prairie provinces object to-and this applies to the maritimes as well-is that the freight rate discrimination against the economies of two sections of Canada is being perpetuated and the unfair discriminatory rates that have continued over the years are being added to. By 1922 the normal level of freight rates in the western provinces was 15 per cent above that of Ontario and Quebec. So far as the Crowsnest rates are concerned, I join with the hon. member for Regina City, as I have done on many occasions in this house, in urging the maintenance of those rates. There is no question about that so far as members from any of the western provinces are concerned, regardless of political considerations. That is old straw. All are in favour of those rates and intend to press that they are maintained. No matter what political party one belongs to, if from western Canada you support those rates. I am surprised that the hon. member for Regina City did not raise his voice against the injustice of this increase coming as it does on top of the increase in March.
On a question of privilege, I raised my voice against it. I clearly stated that I called upon the government to prevent this injustice taking place.
All right. Now that we have the voice let us also have the vote to support the voice.
On another question of privilege, the vote will follow the voice-
All right.
-but I will interpret it.
Mr. Chairman, in effect he says, I shall do evil and call it good.
The hon. member usually does.
Of course that is no reply.
Nobody knows that better than the hon. member.

I am going to call as my witness the Saskatchewan Liberal party and a resolution that they supported in the provincial legislature a few weeks ago. I

Supply-Transport
will also call as my witness a member of the government, Stuart Garson, the then premier of Manitoba.
Hear, hear.

His was a voice for the western people when he was in the west, but that voice has not been raised since coming to the House of Commons. The voice that we used to hear from the premier of Manitoba, as he then was, is still. Oh for the sound of that voice once more-in parliament, where it would have the power to effect what it advocated in the legislature of Manitoba.
Hear, hear.

I want to read from the resolution that was introduced in the Saskatchewan legislature on March 7, 1950, as reported in the Regina Leader-Post. I shall quote the Regina Leader-Post and the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix as well later on on the question of freight rates to show that this is a matter that knows no disunity of opinion among western Canadians, regardless of party consideration. In view of the fact that discrimination is taking place and is intensified by horizontal increases, the continuation of freight rates at their present level strikes at the economy of the western farmer and farmers of the maritimes as well. It strikes at the expansion of industry in western Canada as it does also in the maritimes. The horizontal increases have been imposed on the original unfair discriminatory rates of 15 per cent and as a result the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan are now paying 21-78 per cent higher freight rates than are paid in the two central provinces of Ontario and Quebec. It was 15 per cent three or four years ago, and by reason of the horizontal increases the difference is now 21-78 per cent.
There was no division of opinion when the matter came before the Saskatchewan legislature on the 7th of March. There was a united front. The Minister of Transport must have received the resolution passed unanimously by the legislature and calling upon the federal government to act. The minister indicated today that the government cannot act and terminated his speech by saying in effect that with the case now sub judice and on its way to the privy council, in his opinion the increases were justified. That is not the attitude for a minister of the crown to take on a matter before the courts, thereby indicating that the government approves what has been done.
It is not a question of the railways' need for more income. If extra income is needed and rates must be increased no one will object, but what we do object to is that by

continuing to allow these increases, which have the result of increasing the discrimination against the western provinces and the maritimes. Precedent is piling on precedent until finally we will find ourselves in the position where we are discriminated out of existence, economically speaking. That is why there was no division of opinion in the Saskatchewan legislature on the 7th day of March. The motion was passed by all members. It was supported by Mr. Walter Tucker, K.C., leader of the Liberal party in Saskatchewan, in language that I am going to place upon the record of the house. The report in the Regina Leader-Post of March 7, 1950, reads:
A resolution calling on the federal government to disallow the recent 16 per cent freight rate increase pending completion of the report of the royal commission on transportation was given unanimous endorsation by the legislature Monday. Speaking in its support were Premier T. C. Douglas, opposition leader Walter Tucker and municipal affairs minister L. F. McIntosh.
The resolution read: "That this assembly strongly protests the recent increases in freight rates granted by the board of transport commissioners, and requests the Saskatchewan government to appeal the decision to the federal government, urging the said government to exercise its statutory power of disallowance under section 52 of the Railway Act, disallowing the latest increases pending the report of the royal commission on transportation."
That was not a Conservative motion. It was a motion moved in the legislature of Saskatchewan. Mr. Douglas pointed out that the increase in March and the recent increases during the past two years had resulted in the consumers of Canada having to pay an additional $131 million in freight rates. The amount has now been increased to approximately $144 million. Mr. Douglas is reported as saying:
We can be sure a heavy share of this burden fell on the people of the west and maritimes where lack of competition has allowed the railways to take full advantage of horizontal increases.
Further on:
"We propose to carry the matter to the federal government and ask them to disallow the 16 per cent increase under the veto power in section 52 of the Railway Act." . . . Opposition leader Walter Tucker complimented the premier for bringing forward a resolution on which there could be no political differences.
It is not very often you have compliments passing between those two gentlemen, but all difficulties were forgotten in the face of the needs of that province and the feelings of the people as a whole. Mr. Tucker had this to say in part:
"On this question of protecting the people of Saskatchewan from bearing an unfair share of railway freight increases the government has the determined and united support of the Liberal opposition. The government of Canada, having committed itself to the setting up of a royal commission

on transportation, must know that we are not going to let any increase come into effect until we get the findings of that commission."
There was the leader of the Liberal party in the province of Saskatchewan taking a most definite stand. He went on to say something more, and these are not my directions to the minister; they come from his former colleague in this house, now the leader of his party in Saskatchewan, who said:
The governor general in council was under no obligation, he believed-
That is Mr. Tucker.
-to permit the latest increase as long as it was not consistent with the over-all policy of the federal government.
In other words, in effect Mr. Tucker said there should be disallowance unless it was the view of the federal government that the discriminatory situation should be permitted to continue. Then he said something more; and while my own words may have no effect I should think the words of Mr. Tucker should be most effective in reply to those who take a different stand from that taken by the province of Saskatchewan. He said:
"There is no reason why the west should bear all the extra costs of a railroad system that is essential to the whole nation." It was also because of national tariff policy, he pointed out, that western Canada had to ship most of its goods from central Canada.
"These factors had left an economic gap between central Canada and the west, Mr. Tucker said, and in their brief to the board of transport commissioners the western provinces had established an 'unanswerable case' in favour of a national subsidy to close the gap."
Then he went on to set forth the situation in general, at considerable length. At that time he expressed the first and fundamental objection to this increase which is that it has the effect of intensifying the injustice that has prevailed over the years. We used to object when the rate was 15 per cent higher in western Canada than in Ontario and Quebec. Surely now we have a right to object when that difference has been increased by approximately 6-8 per cent. This latest increase, coupled with the previous increases, in time will have the result of crippling our western economy. Why should it be brought in at this time, with the Turgeon commission just having concluded its sittings, heard the argument and commenced to consider its report? Surely this piling on of discrimination against the western and maritime provinces should be discontinued. As far as I can see the government can advance no argument for disregarding the call from Macedonia by Mr. Tucker, when he said in effect "Disallow these increases or you will do harm to the economy of the prairie provinces".
Well, Mr. Chairman, there is another voice, that of the Minister of Justice, a clarion
Supply-Transport
voice with which he used to call upon the western provinces to preserve their birthright against injustice. I read first from the Manitoba submission opposing any increase in freight rates, presented to the board of transport commissioners during the hearing of the application for a 30 per cent increase, in 1947. I am quoting from appendix C, "Submission by Premier Stuart Garson," in which he said:
May I, at this point, briefly recapitulate:
The prairie provinces are in the centre of Canada's railway system.
They are a heavy producer of export goods and a heavy consumer of Canadian manufactured goods.
They therefore provide the railways with their longest and most profitable type of freight haul.
They therefore are most adversely affected by a freight rate increase because they have to pay both coming and going over long hauls.
The prairie provinces already pay a disproportionate share of the cost of railway operation in Canada.
That was in 1947. Since then the rates have been increased by more than 40 per cent; but even in 1947 the premier of Manitoba said that the prairie provinces already paid a disproportionate share of the cost of railway operation in Canada. Surely, belonging to a government that has power to act, the voice of the crusader in 1947 should be translated into the actions of the statesman of 1950. Now I shall read from the foreword, also written by the present Minister of Justice, dated January 5, 1948, in which he sets out the facts in such a way that they cannot be challenged. Those facts were accepted by the province of Saskatchewan, as well as by Manitoba. This is what he said:
Since the early days of railroad construction in western Canada, Manitoba has always been in the forefront of those who have opposed the efforts of the railways to take advantage of their quasimonopolistic position in the prairies by imposing high freight rates which must be paid by the people of western Canada because they have no alternative transportation for the great bulk of the commodities which they buy and sell. Most of the people of western Canada are farmers, miners, fishermen and other raw material producers, or those whose interests are closely tied to this kind of primary production. This is the very group which would be harmed the most by high freight rates.
Let me repeat that statement:
This is the very group which would be harmed the most by high freight rates. For example, in the case of livestock products the return to the western farmer is the price at the market less the cost of getting the article to the market. On the other hand, in the case of manufactured goods, the manufacturer in eastern Canada, because of his tariff protection, is able to sell in western Canada at a price which is set by his factory price in eastern Canada plus the ccfst of shipping goods from the factory to the user. Thus, high freight rates are a burden upon western Canada both coming and going.
In view of these facts of economics and geography, the people of western Canada have always been quick to oppose any proposal that freight

rates should he increased. Consequently, when on October 9, 1946, the Railway Association of Canada applied for authority to raise freight rates by 30 per cent with certain exceptions, Manitoba was quick to express its opposition and to prepare to state its position before the authorities charged with the responsibility of deciding the matter.
I shall read one further paragraph, in which the present Minister of Justice went on to say:
However, if residents of Manitoba paid that proportion of the increased cost of shipments in the western provinces that Manitoba's population bears to the population of the western provinces, then the additional cost to Manitoba resulting from a 30 per cent increase in freight rates would be over $800,000 per month or $9J million per year.
So that there be no mistake that we were discriminated against in 1947, and that our freight rates were so much higher than in eastern Canada, I quote these words from the Minister of Justice:
They have shown-
That is Manitoba and these provinces that were opposing these increases.
-that the average level of all effective freight rates is higher by at least fourteen per cent in the west than in the east and that although the total amounts spent for working expenses in the two areas are almost identical, nevertheless, profits in the west exceed profits in the east in the ratio of 2 to 1.
It is a tremendously important submission that was made, and it was supported by the outstanding leaders in agriculture in the province of Manitoba as well as the province of Saskatchewan. It is for that reason, sir, I ask the Minister of Transport not to treat this matter in the way he did this morning, as though nothing could be done. I do not believe in the political fixation of freight rates, but I do believe if we are to build a united Canada there cannot be two, three, or four different kinds of citizenship, according to the freight rate structure in the several parts of Canada. You cannot build a united Canada on the basis of freight rates that are unjust to some sections of the country. That is why this matter becomes of such transcendent importance. I repeat that this last increase, coupled with the other increases, means that the western provinces will be paying 21-78 per cent higher freight rates than are being paid in Ontario and Quebec. This cannot continue; the problem must be determined. The commission has been sitting, and while the commission sits to determine whether discrimination shall be allowed, the discrimination continues to mount.
I shall now read, sir, from the Winnipeg Free Press editorials on this subject. It has taken a very strong stand over the years. On March 3, 1950, that newspaper said this: This discrimination in rates is an old, old story, being the pith and substance of almost every major 
freight rate case since 1907. Some forty years of consistent and unremitting effort on the part of the western provinces has gone into the fight for justice in freight rates.
The discrimination arises as follows:
The editorial sets out what the result is, and then it points out:
Up to 1922, the transport board repeatedly moved to correct this discrimination by granting larger increases in rates in the east than in the west or by granting an increase in the east but none in the west.
Since 1922 the board of transport commissioners has done nothing such as it did prior to 1922 to prevent the increase in degree of discrimination. The article continues:
Thus the old discrimination against the west not only remains but is worsened1. The latest flat increase of 7-4 per cent applied to an eastern rate of, say, 85 cents is one thing. Applied to a western rate on the identical commodity of one dollar, it is another. The present differential of 15 per cent is increased.
When I hear praise of the transport board, these words come to me from the Winnipeg Free Press:
The opinion of the west will be that once again the transport board has been derelict in its duty to the detriment of this part of Canada.
These are not the words of a Conservative paper; these are not the words of the opposition in parliament; these are the words of the Winnipeg Free Press which, over the years, has fought a battle on behalf of the removal of the unjustly discriminatory system that has prevailed for years, and has been intensified in recent years. When the Minister of Justice was in Manitoba his freight rate conscience reposed in the Free Press. I ask him to bring to bear on the government to which he now belongs the force of the principles which he enunciated in 1947. They are even more true today, because the discrimination of that day has been added to by horizontal increases.
What should our attitude be? The attitude in Saskatchewan is shown by the editorials in every newspaper in that province. The Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of May 26 said this:
The board of transport commissioners has sanctioned another increase in freight rates. This time it is 3-4 per cent. But coming on top of three other increases in a little more than two years it will inevitably push some farm districts and some businesses in western Canada below the level of profitability.
This newspaper concludes that the increase is going to result in business and farm districts in certain localities being forced below the level of profitability. The editorial continues:
The things we sell and most of the things we buy must move by rail at some stage in their exchange. We have no waterways or other forms of transport

to restrain the insatiable appetite of the railways for more money. The west pays the full shot every time.
At the end of the article, this appears:
The present order perpetuates these errors in rate making. It is the third time these errors have been applied since the cabinet asked for a review. They are in a fair way to becoming established as precedents unless they are challenged. The provinces must appeal this order as they did the order of March 1, 1950. And when the appeal is launched, the government should hear the appeals before the new rate goes into effect. We think the new rate is unjust because it is based on rate-making rules that are unjust. The cabinet is our only remaining protection. We should have access to it immediately before any more damage is done.
Surely that challenges the Minister of Transport to speak otherwise than he did in his concluding words today, when in effect he gave approval to what has been done.
The Regina Leader-Post is equally definite. In an editorial on May 27 it said this:
With the latest award, rates have been increased by 45-2 per cent since 1948 to extract an estimated additional $144 million in revenue from the public. But this will not be the end.
Farther down it says:
The cabinet clearly has the authority to grant a stay in the application of the higher rates. The appeal already has been made to the cabinet following the March 1 award. But consideration was postponed until the board had completed its judgment on the application which was disposed1 of Thursday.
Then the editorial gives this reason for postponement until the report of this royal commission is brought down:
Since the main purpose in appointing the Turgeon commission was to endeavour to find a remedy for this situation, the fair and sensible course for the cabinet to take is to grant the provinces' appeals in the hope that shortly the commission's report will point a way to a solution of this knotty problem.
Sir, no matter where one goes in the western provinces, whatever the political faith may be of the individual, farmers and businessmen are saying, as I know the maritime people are saying, that because we live on the western plains, by reason of geographical location, this discrimination must cease. There is very little hope of its being stopped when the minister approaches the subject in the offhand, cavalier way he did this morning. He gave us history. It is- not history they want today. What they want is action. He places the responsibility directly upon the board of transport commissioners.
There is only one means by which the leader of the opposition could bring this matter to the attention of the country, and that is by the traditional method. I could go into the records of the old country to show where the same method has been used on occasion. Where there are boards, and the government takes the recommendations of 55946-1991

the boards and has the power to disallow them and does not, the only way in which parliament can speak is through an amendment reducing the expenditure for the board in question to the sum of one dollar. That is the only way in which members of parliament can officially say-I speak for those in the western provinces-whether or not they accept what has been done.
It is all very well to say, when the session of parliament is over and we go home, that we were against the increase. It is so easy to say that. There is no other way. If anybody can tell me of any other way by which parliament can show that we from the western provinces and the other provinces of Canada are discriminated against, that we oppose this discrimination, that we do not believe an injustice can be removed by aggravating an existing discrimination, I will give him an opportunity to do so.
This debate is one which directly affects men and women everywhere in this dominion. As I said at the beginning, no one argues the need of private enterprise being able to pay a fair and reasonable return; no one argues that you want to see perpetuated a system whereby any government industry is constantly coming back to parliament for help. Fair rates will assure fair wages; proper rates will assure the discharge of the proper responsibilities in expenditure. But surely the answer to the railway problem of Canada is not to load discrimination on top of discrimination against certain areas within our country.
I could go further and quote from the present Minister of Justice when he was premier of Manitoba, who said in 1947 that if the eastern rates were raised to the equivalent of what the then western rates were any question of a deficit would be done away with. Whether that is the solution I am not saying. That is what the Turgeon commission is endeavouring to decide at the present time. Since the matter is before the commission I am asking through you, sir, that the minister shall heed the small voice-it must be small today because no one has heard it-of the Minister of Justice who, speaking in stentorian tones in 1947, said in effect, "This condition dare not continue." And since then it has not only continued but multiplied and increased while the minister has sat as a member of the cabinet.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few observations to make in this debate. I have listened with much interest to what has been said so far. In my opinion, what we are considering at this time is, first, whether the board of transport commissioners is competent or otherwise; second, whether the

A royal commission is looking into the problem; but before I go into the details of a discussion of that kind I should like to say this to the hon. member for Regina City-he invited it. When he was speaking he made some critical observations with regard to what the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar had to say this morning, and intimated that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar was departing from the position that he had taken on this question over the years.
I thought the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar was clear -this morning. His whole protest was based on the inequality that exists with respect to freight rates as between the centre, the east and the west. The hon. member for Regina City charged that the deficits on the Canadian National Railways accrue particularly because of the increases in wages.
On a point of privilege, I named no railroad.

The hon. member's observations would not leave any doubt in anyone's mind.
Mr. Gauthier (Porineufk That is your opinion.
First, he is wrong in the statement that the deficit on the Canadian National Railways accrues because of wages.
Once again, on personal privilege, I made no such statement, nor did I insinuate it.
The Canadian National is the only railway that has a deficit. The hon. member could not be talking about any other.

Mr. Chairman, I was not speaking of deficits. The statement which I did make-and the hon. member would have heard it had he been listening-was that the railroads had stated that the allowable increase in freight rates had been taken up by increases in wages. I said nothing of deficits.
The hon. member did make reference to the wage demands that are now before the different railroads, and so forth.
The hon. member will see it in Hansard.
He has already made the statement, and he can read it tomorrow or correct it tonight, if he wants to.
I am not in the habit of doing that.

A member who, during a debate has spoken to a question may again be heard to offer explanation of some material part of his speech which has been misunderstood; but he must not introduce new matter or endeavour to strengthen by new arguments, his former position which he alleges to have been misunderstood, or to reply to other members. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I
hope the hon. member understands that. I listened with a lot of patience to him while he made the statement, and did not interrupt him.
Of course, the propaganda that wage rates are responsible for all difficulties and deficits in every industry is not something new. I have heard it for the last thirty years, and it has been very prominent recently in the press. Editorial after editorial, chambers of commerce and so forth have been driving it home to the public. I am not surprised that my hon. friend fell for it. That is not the case, however. I think it is nearly time everyone understood that. I am thinking in terms of the Canadian National Railways, because I am particularly interested in them-and I suggest every member in the committee should be.
In the final analysis this whole question is not the responsibility of the board of transport commissioners or of any royal commission. The final responsibility rests with this House of Commons-and I say we should understand that. I would like to look at both

sides of this question. The railways render a public service and must be maintained, and in order to operate they must have money. The only place they can get money is from those who patronize the system. Let me say this, for the benefit of anyone who has not been looking into the operations of the C.N.R. particularly, that it has not been wages that have pulled them down, nor has it been ordinary operating costs which have brought about deficits.
Every year the Canadian National starts out with a deficit of $45 million in interest charges on loans from the government in respect of the bonds of old, defunct railroads that should have been called in and liquidated years ago. That $45 million about which we hear so much in the press and in the House of Commons should be understood. It does not accrue because of operating inefficiency or because of the wage debt but rather from fixed interest charges on dead services. The capital should be written off as interest-bearing capital and show in the books as equity capital, or it should be called in and written off altogether. I hope when hon. members are considering that feature of the system they will keep this debt load in mind.
Later on I shall deal with freight rates as such. However, let me speak briefly now on the question as to whether the board of transport commissioners is a competent body. As a result of the debates I have heard in the house respecting freight rates since 1945, setting out how the whole question has been handled, I would say there is something lacking in the personnel of that body.
A return in the name of the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Hatfield) to which reference was made this morning by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), gives the names of the members of the board, and their previous occupations. I have not anything against anyone on the board, or any particular occupation; but I say that a body selected to handle the very difficult problem of fixing freight rates in Canada and of doing all the work the board has to do should consist of personnel highly trained for that position.
I shall not put any names on record. Hon. members may look at the document to which I have referred and they will find among the occupations listed there many lawyers, an undertaker, a real estate agent, car dealers and stenographers. Those particular callings do not give the qualifications, in my opinion, to handle a job of that kind.
Then, according to the return, the freight rate experts are all ex-employees of either the C.N.R. or the C.P.R. I do not know whether they are still working for those organizations. I think however it is the
Supply-Transport
responsibility of the minister not to appoint a royal commission; if the board of transport commissioners are competent there should not have been a royal commission. If the personnel of the board had been selected carefully with full regard for their qualifications, and appointed on their merits, there should have-been no necessity to hire a royal commission- because the board is a royal commission, sitting continuously and reporting through the minister to the government.
Why should we at this late date, when we have got into this tangle about freight rates, have to go out and hire another body to examine into the organization that is supposed to be efficient and competent and equipped to deal with this matter from day to day? It does not make sense. No; there should not be a royal commission; but I think the minister's department should make a job valuation survey of the (board of transport commissioners, and take a look at the qualifications of the personnel. There are not too many of them; probably there are not enough. I believe there should be an examination of the qualifications of everyone on the board who has anything to do with the problems they have to handle. I believe there is ample justification for the accusation that they are not competent-at least they have not shown, to date, that they are.
Then, secondly, is there justification for the rates asked for? Taking a look at both sides of the question, and as one of the members who served on the committee on government-owned railways and shipping, and as one who had a chance to take a look at the balance sheet and to examine witnesses, from Mr. Gordon down, let me say that in my opinion, so far as the management of the Canadian National Railways is concerned-I do not know anything about the C.P.R., so I am not, going to talk about it-they are as efficient as could be found in this country. I believe-that in Mr. Gordon they have a man who is very competent and very determined to do-something about the disabilities of the system over which he presides. He has shown a clear grasp of the problem, and I think we have noquarrel so far as the management of the Canadian National Railways is concerned.
If we examine the justification for the freight rates, from the standpoint of the present financial position, they are justified. But, as I intimated earlier, the C.N.R. is in a false position; and unless we are able to correct that position by bringing about some adjustment in the capital structure of the national railways, we are going to continue to go on and on in this way-there will be no end to it.

My opinion is that in respect of these freight rates for the C.N.R. and C.P.R., and their relationship to the whole economic set-up of the country, as well as to other industrial aspects of the problem, we are entering upon a new economic age. This country has reached the point where the old yardstick by which we measured things is no longer good enough. We have to do a lot of serious thinking and make a good many serious revisions in the whole economic structure of Canada, of which this is only one part.
The western part of this country has ample justification for complaining about the inequality of freight rates and the discrimination resulting therefrom. The maritimes also have ample justification for the same complaints. The 21 per cent increase in freight rates that was to be applied straight across the board was, to the best of my knowledge, never applied in Ontario-and if it was applied in Quebec, only to a limited extent. But it applied 100 per cent both east and west, The centre has direct competition, and their hauls are short, but in other parts of the country both east and west that is not so. On everything going either to the east or to the west, from the centre, higher rates were applied; on everything going out the same rates applied. Perhaps 80 per cent of the freight goes into those provinces and adds to consumer costs. Very little is shipped out of the maritimes except raw materials. It hits those who are shipping out, but the ultimate cost is passed on to the consumer. I submit that there is ample justification for the complaint that has been made.
No recommended solution has been offered so far by hon. members who have spoken, and I am going to make a few recommendations which are based upon the thinking of the people of the maritimes. There are one or two things I should like to clear up. Many people in central Canada consider that the maritimes are receiving a rebate or subsidy under the Maritime Freight Rates Act. I notice that some of the people appearing before the royal commission referred to that as a subsidy. I should like to put the record straight on that particular point.
The 20 per cent that is allowed under the Maritime Freight Rates Act is not a subsidy. In 1912 there was a general increase in freight rates of 55 per cent, but when that was applied to the maritimes it amounted to 92 per cent. We suffered under that injustice until the early twenties when the Duncan royal commission on maritime rights recommended that a 20 per cent rebate should be paid under the Maritime Freight Rates Act. We are still 17 per cent worse off than the rest of the country on a percentage basis. An
[Mr. Gillis.l
injustice was perpetuated under the terms of confederation and they still owe us 17 per cent on freight rates. I do not want to hear anyone calling it a subsidy because it is simply part payment of something that is owing to us and for which we are still pressing.
Unless recommendations are made there is not much to fasten to, and I should like to refer to some that have been made in the maritimes. They may not be all right, but also they may not be all wrong. I think the committee may be able to get something from them. These recommendations were put forward by the New Brunswick government and by the maritime transportation commission. By the way, that body has a very good grasp of the whole transportation problem across this country, including freight rates. The recommendations that were made were as follows:
1.	Lessen the impact of percentage-type freight rate increases-the kind awarded the railways since the war-on the long haul traffic typical of the maritimes.
2.	Restore rate relationships existing between Canadian ocean ports before the last series of increases.
3.	Preserve advantages guaranteed under the Maritime Freight Rates Act of 1927, which it is claimed have been partly nullified by transportation changes since then.
4.	Extend the application of the act to make its statutory rate reductions effective on rail-and-water shipments from points in the maritimes to those outside the area.
In addition New Brunswick went a step further and asked for a 50 per cent increase in the rates under the Maritime Freight Rates Act and a wider coverage as to traffic to which it would be applicable. That statute now provides for a 20 per cent rebate on rail traffic within the maritimes and on the maritimes part of westbound traffic originating in those provinces. New Brunswick asks that the rebate be increased by 30 per cent and that it apply on the maritimes section of eastbound traffic into the maritimes from points outside.
Were those recommendations made to the royal commission?

Yes. There was some disagreement as to the last point on the ground that it might interfere with fair competition. I do not think that argument is valid because we do not manufacture anything in the maritimes that would be in competition with anything manufactured in Ontario or Quebec. As I said before, most of our exports are raw materials and our young people. Despite the fact that certain sections of the press disagreed with that recommendation, I believe it should receive consideration.

Prince Edward Island went a bit further and advocated the nationalization of the whole Canadian transportation system. I am not going to comment on that; I shall give Premier Jones an opportunity to explain what he means some time in the future. I believe that a solution is to be found in the submission by the president of the Canadian National Railways to the royal commission on transportation. Mr. Gordon summed it up very well when he asked that, there be a revamping of the capital structure of the system, a writing-off of the $45 million of fixed interest charges which the system is now carrying. I believe that if that were done, with the present management the system could be made efficient and in the future could be taken as the yardstick to be used. Unless that is done I do not know how the system can struggle along.
Last year the press was full of stories about the deficit of $42 million which the Canadian National Railways had incurred, but then elsewhere you would read that they had an operating profit of some $4 million. It is hard to understand these different editorials, one saying they had a profit of $4 million and the next one saying they had a deficit of $42 million. The people just do not understand that sort of thing.
I sat in this house as a member for a long time and voted for bills to wipe out deficits year after year. For a long time I thought that those were accumulated deficits from the previous year's operations, but then I began to dig through the books and finally found out the size of the load the system was carrying. I think it is rather unreasonable and unrealistic for the government to lend money to the Canadian National Railways and then have the system pay an interest charge of around $21 million a year. We pass a bill for $45 million, it goes to the C.N.R. and they pay back $21 million to the government. The principal is still there and goes on and on.
Old railroads representing $24 million in fixed interest charges were taken over. Under ordinary circumstances those roads would have gone into bankruptcy, but they were loaded on the Canadian National system. The bonds were transferred and the Canadian National carries all that deadwood, representing lines that produced practically no revenue, on which they pay a fixed interest charge of $24 million a year. It just does not make sense.
I do not think the proponents of free enterprise would expect that any free enterprise carrying on in that way can make money. I presume most hon. members are familiar with Mr. Gordon's submission to the royal commission on transportation. What it boils
Supp ly-Transport
down to is that he simply asks them to do what I am suggesting. He asks the commission to take into consideration the possibility of taking the bonds and government loans and, instead of showing them on the balance sheet as interest-bearing bonds and loans, show them as equity capital bearing no interest, or that on the other hand the government should take a look at the whole thing, try to write it off and start the system off again with a clean sheet. Unless that is done, in my opinion freight rates will continue to go up. There is no way out of it unless we revamp the Canadian National system.
I think if we did so it would create stiff competition for the Canadian Pacific Railway, which would be a good thing for the country. It is my opinion that in the past a lot of the business that should have gone to the Canadian National has been deliberately swung in the other direction. I have noticed a proposal that freight from the maritimes should be shipped through Moncton to Saint John to the Canadian Pacific line, from there through the United States to Montreal, and that the provisions of the Maritime Freight Rates Act be applied. That cannot be done. The Maritime Freight Rates Act is not applicable unless it is a through haul. In addition it would just mean swinging more business from the C.N.R. to the C.P.R.
I do not want to be dogmatic about the question because my knowledge of it is not too great. I want to see the right thing done. I am absolutely sure in my own mind that, unless the C.N.R. can be relieved of the great debt it has been carrying since its inception, by revamping the whole capital structure, so far as the Canadian freight rate question is concerned we are going to go through the same thing year after year. As the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar pointed out this morning, the future development of Canada depends on the railroad system. Unless it is efficiently maintained and properly routed throughout the country it is not possible to develop either the north or the south, the east or the west. We must have a good efficient transportation system.
I think we have an efficient transportation system. I do not think there is any better in the world. I know that since the war there has been a great improvement in rolling stock, and efforts are being made to repair lines. I know that in the maritimes, where it is badly needed, some work is being done. The Minister of Transport is pushing very strongly for the bridge across the strait of Canso. That is a part of the Canadian National system and will be of great importance to that section of the country. I had

Supply-Transport
the privilege of attending the meetings of the sessional committee on the operations of the Canadian National Railways for four or five weeks and investigating their business. I believe the management is doing everything it can to bring about more economic operation and better service for the Canadian people. It is our job to help them. I was glad to see that the committee, after going over the whole structure of the C.N.R., inserted in its report to the house a recommendation that the government should seriously consider, along the lines suggested by Mr. Gordon, the complete revision of the whole capital structure.
I come to the amendment of the leader of the opposition. My view is that if it is passed it means the end of the board of transport commissioners. If you cut their money completely they cannot work. Nobody works for nothing. At the same time I believe a protest to the board of transport commissioners is in order as to the way in which they handled the whole freight rate question. When the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar was speaking this morning he stated that he did not think we could move an amendment to the amendment. Our technical expert on Beau-chesne was absent at the time. The hon. member for Kootenay West substituted for him. He is much slower but he finally found a citation in the second edition of Beauchesne that would justify us in moving an amendment to the amendment, and I propose to do so at this time. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar:
That the amendment be amended by striking out the word "to" and substituting therefor the word "by."
The amended amendment would then read:
That item 524 of the estimates of the Department of Transport be reduced by one dollar.
I notice that my ecclesiastical friend over here thinks I am wrong in saying "by". The leader of the opposition said "to one dollar". That would mean we would be wiping out all the money which would enable the board of transport commissioners to carry on its operation. The amendment to the amendment says, "by one dollar". That will not hurt them very much but at the same time it is a protest against the way in which the whole freight rate question was handled.
A mild protest.

Many hon. members will say that they cannot vote to wipe out the board of transport commissioners but anyone who is interested in protesting can vote for the amendment to the amendment because it

merely means that they will be voting in protest against the way the whole freight rate question was handled.
Make it $1.50.

I merely want to re-emphasize that, in my opinion, if members of the house want to do something about freight rates and prevent this kind of discussion in the future the only way they can do so is to get behind Mr. Donald Gordon's program for the complete revision of the capital structure of the Canadian National Railways.

I want to say a word by way of explanation. I think the hon. member for Cape Breton South misunderstood what I said this morning. I made no protest about increased wages. I merely expressed surprise that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, in supporting the amendment of the leader of the opposition, should be so inconsistent as to protest that freight rate increases are too great and should not be granted. By so doing he was objecting to wage increases. In effect that is what he did. I know we all agree that the disparity in rates should not be allowed to exist. I quoted from an editorial in the Winnipeg Free Press to show what was being claimed. The editorial reads:
The extent to which the Canadian people paid for the past wage increases, in the form of higher freight rates, can easily be shown. During the war, price ceilings prevented the railways from raising rates to counterbalance the increased costs, mainly in wages, of wartime. But with the lifting of the ceilings the railways launched their campaign. In October, 1946, they applied for an increase in freight rates of 30 per cent.
This is what will interest the hon. member for Cape Breton South.
After a battle that lasted for eighteen months, the board of transport commissioners awarded them an increase of 21 per cent, costing the public about $70 million a year. But all this was immediately sucked away by the wage increase of 1948 which cost $73 million a year.
I referred to no railroad.
May I ask what you are reading from?

It is from page 3 of a reprint of editorials in the Winnipeg Free Press in April and May, 1950. The reprint is entitled, "The Railway Wage Dispute". I then asked, "Is he opposed to giving the brotherhood of railway workers an increase in wages?" That was my statement this morning; and I thank you, Mr. Chairman, for giving me an opportunity to correct the hon. member.

May I also have a moment to make my position clear. My whole speech

this morning was directed against discrimination in freight rates. As far as wages are concerned, in the course of my remarks I pointed out that many thousands of low paid railway workers were suffering from the high cost of living, and I went on to say that if the railways could not operate economically we should integrate our transportation system and if necessary subsidize the railways. I was not changing my position in any respect, as my hon. friend suggests.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to express a few thoughts on this subject before this discussion concludes. I was disappointed indeed in the remarks of the Minister of Transport this afternoon. He gave a fairly good resume of the applications of the railways for increased rates, but certainly he did not indicate any solution whatever for the problem facing this country, except to agree with the tremendous increase of some 45 per cent that has been granted. In effect he also agreed with the increased discrimination which has been created against the maritimes and the prairie provinces. He agrees with the continuation of this discrimination, which is making it very difficult for people in those areas to maintain themselves. The unfair differential in freight rates has placed the western provinces in a very serious position. Therefore I must agree entirely with the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition.
I am not quite so sure as the hon. member for Cape Breton South that the board of transport commissioners is so efficient; therefore I am not so enthusiastic about supporting his subamendment. I must say I have not very much confidence in a board which, having been in existence for so long and having investigated this problem so thoroughly, has permitted this great discrimination to continue for all these years. Particularly does my confidence in the board fail in the face of these tremendous increases in freight rates, which have been permitted in spite of the fact that the western provinces protested so vigorously.
I want to deal with this subject from a little different angle than those who have spoken previously. In my view the railways, as disclosed in their submissions to the royal commission-and I am referring now to the presentation made by the C.P.R.-were not so much interested in solving the difficulties presented by these tremendous increases and this discrimination as in showing that the trucking industry, their only effective competitor in western Canada at least, should be driven out of the field, though by their own actions the railways are pricing themselves 55946-199
Supply-Transport
out of competition. The fact is that they are now attempting to do away with competition and establish a monopoly in the field of transportation, and that is the phase with which I want to deal more particularly this afternoon.
I do not believe anyone would contend for a moment that the railways are not a national asset, or that they should not be kept in a sound position. As has been indicated many times this afternoon, the railways are intended to serve all Canada, and if they are to carry out that function they must be maintained in a strong position. That does not mean, however, that the railways should be maintained in a favoured position or that they should be permitted to drive out their only competitors and have the field to themselves. As I pointed out on another occasion in this house the people in central Canada have more or less effective competition in the form of water transportation. Even those living in British Columbia obtain the benefits of water competition. Rail rates are rising so rapidly that General Motors are using the only effective competition against the railways and are sending their automobiles by trailer trucks to Montreal, then by boat through the Panama canal to British Columbia, thereby saving more than $80 per automobile. That is effective competition, and as a result British Columbia is in a position to get a more favourable rate structure than those in the prairie provinces or the maritimes.
The only effective competition we have in western Canada is provided by trucks; and in their presentations to the royal commission the railways did everything they could to get rid of that competition. As a matter of fact the greater part of their presentations was directed to that point. One must not take the position that the railways are a private enterprise, for such is not the case. My remarks apply particularly to the C.P.R., and I would point out that the greater part of the presentation to the royal commission was made by that company. They were the puppets who were carrying the ball for the Canadian National and the government, so it was up to them to make the presentation, which they did somewhat reluctantly. These railways have not built themselves up to their present position solely by their own efforts. I think hon. members of this house should be reminded of that. A great deal of assistance has been given to the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National as well.
In 1873 there was a grant of 50 million acres of land to the Canadian Pacific. The

Supp ly-Transp ort
oil and mineral rights went along with that grant, and will become extremely profitable before very long. On top of that land grant, as the member for Rosetown-Biggar pointed out this afternoon, there were tremendous cash grants given to both the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National. These railways have been built up to their present status by these large grants of land and cash. In addition to that, the railways have received a large amount in subsidies. I should like to refer to subsidies for a moment. I am not against the principle of subsidizing the railways where necessary. I am just using this as an illustration to show that the railways have been subsidized to a great extent. There is a subsidy on one commodity which they use, and that is coal.
I have in my hand, Mr. Chairman, a report from the Canadian coal board. It gives a breakdown of the subsidies on coal received by the Canadian Pacific. With the permission of the house I should like to put this memorandum on Hansard, but before I do so I want to refer to it. These are the subvention payments made to the Canadian Pacific railway. In the calendar year 1939, there was no breakdown on coal for the railway's use, nor was there a breakdown on coal for domestic and industrial use. The total amount paid that year was $954,765.35. In the year 1940 there was no breakdown under those headings I have mentioned, and the total amount paid was $1,005,386.51. In 1941 there was no breakdown, but the total was $1,505,576.03. In 1942 there was no breakdown, but the total was $1,051,168.01. For 1943 there was no breakdown, but the total was $125,018.93. In 1944 there was a breakdown, and the subsidy paid to the Canadian Pacific on coal for their own use was $15,238.21; for domestic and industrial use it was $62,905.49, making a total of $78,143.70. In 1945, on coal for the railway's use the subsidy amounted to $97,997.83; on coal for domestic and industrial use it was $570,709.81, making a total for the year of $668,707.64. In 1946, on coal for railway use it was $156,752.55; on coal for domestic and industrial use, $577,736.08, making a total of $734,488.63. In 1947, on coal for railway use, it was $13,819.72; on coal for domestic and industrial use, $188,353.32, making a total of $202,173.04. In 1948, on coal for railway use it was $29,611.16; on coal for domestic and industrial use, it was $187,901.39, making a total of $219,512.55. This gives a total subsidy on coal for railway use at the end of 1948 of $313,619.47; on coal for domestic and industrial use, $1,487,606.09, making a total of $6,443,140.39.
This may seem to toe a tremendous amount, but I am going to give the figures for 1949 
to show how these subsidies to the Canadian Pacific have increased. The railway has been receiving a subsidy on coal for its own use, thus lowering its cost of operation. I do not know of any other industry to which a subsidy is granted to lower its cost of operation. May I say that these 1949 figures are subject to adjustment, because the board tells me the final figure is not available as yet, but this is as close to being accurate as they can get at the moment. The subsidy on coal for the railway's own use in this last year amounted to $231,642.56; on coal for domestic and industrial use, $233,975.09, making a total of $465,617.65. It will be noticed that the subsidy paid to the Canadian Pacific for hauling coal for domestic and industrial use was just about the same amount that was paid to the Canadian Pacific for hauling coal for its own use.
Mr. Chairman, before I start another branch of my argument, may I call it six o'clock?
At six o'clock the Speaker resumed the chair and the house took recess.
