"dominion"
The house resumed, from Tuesday, April 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Cote (Matapedia-Matane) for the second reading of Bill No. 4, respecting Canada day.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to say a few words on this bill. As I understand it, the intention of the bill is to change the name of our national day from "Dominion day" to "Canada day". I have heard no real reason given for this change; neither have I heard any definite reason against the idea that would appeal to me. I would prefer to wait until the public mind in the country is more in unison on this particular matter. That is, I would not like to see the name of our national birthday changed without there being unison or practical unanimity in the whole matter.
A year or two ago a similar bill passed this house, but it was killed in the other place. I did not have anything to do with parliament at that time, but I did follow the discussion that took place. The bill met with a considerable amount of opposition in this house, and with almost unanimous opposition in the other place, which is a clear indication to me that public opinion on the question is not close enough to unanimity to justify our passing it at this time, unless there has been a tremendous change in the feeling of the people of the country in the meantime.
So far as I am personally concerned, Mr. Speaker, I would be in favour of the bill if I felt that the people of Canada desired the change. I do not mean a hundred per cent, but if eighty or eighty-five per cent of the people desired this change I would certainly vote for a bill of this kind.
The words "Dominion of Canada", of course, have no legal significance either in the British North America Act or in any other act of this country. In dealing with the matter the British North America Act of 1867 put it this way:
It shall be lawful for the Queen, by and with the advice of Her Majesty's Most Honourable Privy Council, to declare by proclamation that, on and after a day therein appointed, not being more than six months after the passing of this act, the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick shall form and be one dominion under the name of Canada; and on and after that day those three provinces shall form and be one dominion under that name accordingly.
Canada Day
Section 5 reads:
Canada shall be divided into four provinces, named Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.
There is the creation of Canada, not the Dominion of Canada. That was forcibly brought to my attention for the first time, though I never took any particular interest in the matter, on learning that when Sir Robert Borden-and no more staunch Britisher and no greater Canadian ever occupied the proud position of prime minister of this country than the same Sir Robert Borden- came to sign the treaty of Versailles, which was perhaps the first act of a wholly Canadian plenipotentiary, he did not sign it for the Dominion of Canada but for Canada. That was the first time it ever came to my attention that there was no such name by statute or otherwise as the Dominion of Canada.
I could go on and give various other examples of the same thing. However, by statute there is a Dominion day. It was in 1879, I think, that an act of parliament was passed which first introduced Dominion day, and this is the preamble and part of the act:
Whereas it was on the first day of July that the provinces of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick became one dominion under the name of Canada; and
Whereas Rupert's land and the northwestern territory and the province of British Columbia became part of the dominion in the month of July, and Prince Edward Island became part of the dominion on the first day of July; and
Whereas it is expedient that such important events should be commemorated:
Therefore Her Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and the House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows.
Then they created our national holiday, Dominion day. It will be noted that it makes reference there to the Senate and the House of Commons of Canada, not to the Dominion of Canada. As a matter of fact between 1867 and 1879 July 1 had always been commemorated as our national birthday. That was brought to the attention of the house at the time the act was passed, in 1879, by the Hon. David Mills, who said that Dominion day was, he believed, universally kept as a holiday; at least it was in western Canada; but it was not kept under the authority of any act of parliament.
I am not one who thinks that the changing of Dominion day to Canada day would make us any less British or any more Canadian. I do not think it would create any breach in the historic links that join us with the great mother country. I do not think that it would in any way make a breach in the long history of this country, since 1867; nor would it in my humble opinion impress any one

Canada Day
man in this broad dominion with the idea that because this change had taken place we had become less British and more Canadian. I say that because I do not think that we in Canada today can become much more Canadian than we have been for the last thirty, forty or fifty years.
My reason for wishing to see a change in the birthday of Canada is that, notwithstanding the provisions of the British North America Act, I do not think that we are any longer a dominion. We belong to a great commonwealth of nations, and with the same sovereignty I hope-sometimes I doubt it, of course-that the United Kingdom has.
I should think that Confederation day would be a far more appropriate name than would Canada day, and it would also take away any sting from the minds of those who are imbued with the idea that, because we want to call this day Canada day, we are going to be separated from the great mother country.
In this matter there cannot be said to be any flying in the face of tradition. How can we fly in the face of tradition by changing this day? Personally I cannot see how we could. Tradition is something based on a long series of historic events, brought down to us, perhaps not by the written word, but by various acts of omission, and more often acts of commission. These are incorporated into our country, not by the written word but by other means.
There is nothing in the traditions of this country that would be violated by changing the name from Dominion day to Canada day. There is nothing in this change which in any way would tend to separate us further from the great British traditions which we have held in the past and which I hope we shall always hold.
Having in mind that this question might be discussed, during the recess I visited various high schools in the city of Halifax and in my own constituency. On those occasions I discussed with the teachers and pupils in the higher grades this idea of Dominion versus Canada, or Canada versus Dominion. These were intelligent children in the tenth and eleventh grades which, in the old days, was looked upon as a higher educational grading. They knew their history well, although they did not know Canadian history, I am sorry to say, as well as they knew that of foreign countries. When I say that, I mean they did not have a background of the traditional history of this country to the point one might have liked to see. However, I never suggested to these boys and girls why I was discussing the matter with them.

While speaking to them I asked whether they did not feel * it would be better to describe our national birthday as Canada day rather than Dominion day. The general answer seemed to be along this line, "Well, we know what Dominion day is and, in our short lives, we have always celebrated it on July 1. We cannot see why we should now change and call it Canada day." That was the reaction indicated in about three of the schools I visited.
In two other schools, teaching pre-university eleventh and twelfth grades, I found two or three exceptionally bright and intelligent boys who, perhaps, were under a false impression as to the meaning of Empire day. It was their view that if there were going to be any change in the designation of July 1 it should be known as Empire day. I pointed out to them at once that we already had an Empire day. Their reply was that they knew that, but they felt this description of our national birthday would have the effect of cementing the links already existing between Canada and Great Britain.
I may be told that I did not choose a satisfactory source for advice on a matter of this kind. My reply would be that from many of those children I got a good deal of better advice-much of which I am not giving to the house this evening-than I could have given if I had been asked questions on the same subject.
Having regard to what took place in the House of Commons two years ago, and also having regard to the opposition I understand this measure will meet on this oocasion, my impression would be that perhaps we are somewhat premature in attempting to pass the bill. Because, when it comes to a matter of this kind, while it may not have any direct bearing on our relationship with the mother country, there are some aspects of the matter that might be considered in that light. In my view any change we make, whether along patriotic lines or otherwise, in the relations between Canada and the United Kingdom should have behind it a greater approximation to unanimity among members of the House of Commons, and throughout the country. I am in hopes that some time in the future a bill similar to this will meet with the unanimous approval of this house.
I think it was the hon. member for Mata-pedia-Matane (Mr. Cote) who brought this matter to the attention of the house before. At that time he did get the approval of the house. Perhaps I will be pardoned for referring to the debates that took place at that time, but on looking them over it struck me there was a lot of confusion among members who were in the house at that time. I hope I am not insulting anybody when I say that. They seemed to

be at cross purposes. One member would vote for the bill, and you would turn another page and find him voting against it. It seemed to me there was some political prejudice on the part of hon. members, perhaps on both sides of the house, but that would not be the fault of the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane.
That is the stand I take on this bill. If it comes to a vote the probabilities are that I will vote for the bill because I see no reason for voting against it. At the same time I think the bill is premature. The people of this country are not just in a state of mind at the present time to adopt legislation such as this and for that reason I hope the hon. member will withdraw his bill.

Mr. Speaker, I am going to vote
against this bill. I shall not delay the house very long to say what I want to say. Perhaps I can say to the hon. member who has just spoken and to my hon. friend who with the best intentions in the world has moved this motion that there is no more united nation on earth than the Dominion of Canada.

I never suggested anything
else.

I was not referring to my
hon. friend; I was referring to the mover of the motion. I am British in the broadest sense of the word since my grandfather was a Frenchman on my mother's side, and on my father's side Irish. If you want anything better than that, take a look around you. I have travelled throughout the British commonwealth of nations and I have listened to crackpots who talk about empires. I have watched what the British people have done, and I speak again in the broadest sense of the word.
Our people have given the world a system of fairness and decency possessed by no other country since the dawn of history. The other day we listened to the Prime Minister of Pakistan pay a tribute to the family of nations. I think I am one of the few hon. members who have been to Pakistan and I know that tribute was well deserved. We have unity among all the racial groups that go to make up this great dominion. Recently I was in the state of Virginia and I noticed that they still call it the dominion of Virginia and they have a dominion network of radio stations. In Massachusetts where they tossed the tea into the harbour, where they said they would not have taxation without representation, they still call it the commonwealth of Massachusetts.

They had a tea party there.
Canada Day

That may sound strange to
your ears, but they had a tea party. There has been a lot of loose talk about the crown, but I have found that the older you get the more sense you have. Of course some grownup people still believe in fairies and Christmas trees like the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who quoted Brock Chisholm the other day. I liked fairies and Christmas trees when I was a youngster and my children liked them and looked forward to Christmas. I think the world would be better off without the Brock Chisholms.
Hear, hear.

Looking over the world today you find that wherever there is a limited monarchy such as in Sweden, Norway, Holland, Belgium, Denmark and Great Britain you find a regeneration after the devastation of the last war which is unexcelled by most countries. It is one of those things that cannot be explained, but perhaps it is due to the leadership that is given, to the principles of decency that are practised. The crown today in its very essence represents decency in the life of the nation.
I think we are most fortunate in the British commonwealth in having a King and Queen who reflect the best there is in British life. I have often said that the province of my hon. friend may be the sheet anchor of freedom some day in the future.

It is not a
question of talk.
It is a question of common sense.
He has none.

It Is a question of vision, of taking the long view rather than the short view just for political reasons. As I say, that province may some day be the sheet anchor of freedom if things continue to travel the way they may well travel in this very difficult period in which we are living. I simply wanted to pay a tribute to our institutions, to our federal form of government, to our judiciary, to our school system, to our transportation system, to all the great things that this nation has built up in the last four or five hundred years. I say that without any mental reservation whatsoever.
I like the word "dominion". I hope I shall never live to see the day when we do not belong to the great family of nations known as the British commonwealth of nations. Every hon. member knows that during the zenith of its power there was very little trouble in the world. I think the world will be a better place in which to live if we still maintain and insist in this struggle

Canada Day
between two ideologies that the dominions retain their contact with the crown. I am not going into a theoretical exposition of that matter, although I could. I hope the house will vote the motion down. If I am the only member to vote against it I am going to vote against it.
You will have plenty of support.

Like the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) I intend to be very brief. When this bill was before the house a few years ago I voted for it, and I still like the idea. It is also apparent that if the bill were to come to a vote tonight it would in all likelihood be defeated, after the speech just made by the Minister of Labour. It seems to me that there is something to be said for the position that we should not make important changes like this in the one hour allotted to private and public bills, or even in two hours as might be the case considering that this measure was up once before.
On the other hand I always feel uneasy when the result of that argument is that a worthy idea is talked out or defeated altogether. I think the best thing that could be done for this bill and the idea that it contains would be to refer the subject matter to a committee of the house so that it might be discussed further. It is for that purpose that I propose to move the appropriate amendment. Before I do so, may I say that I fully realize the amendment I shall be moving has the effect of suspending any further consideration of the bill itself at this session. Nevertheless it will permit discussion of the subject matter of the bill by the committee to which the subject matter is referred. I can say to the hon. member who is the sponsor of the bill that I was greatly annoyed in 1947 when a bill of mine was treated in this manner, but I must say that in 1948 the subject matter of the bill which was treated that way in 1947 was incorporated in one of the statutes of Canada, namely the federal labour code. Annoying though these procedures may seem at times to the sponsor of a bill, it is not all bad. It can produce discussion and possibly some progress. With that explanation I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge):
That Bill No. 4 be not now read a second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise only to ask you for instruction and assistance. I was on the point of saying what I am about to say before the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) moved the amendment. Point No. 1 is that I do not wish to leave my seat and go into the lobby when the vote comes. Point No. 2 is that I have not any opinion that I consider it worth while to register by voting one way or the other upon either the amendment or the bill itself. I do not really care very much whether we are called "Canada" or "Dominion of Canada". The word "dominion" joined with Canada does not indicate to me dominion over us or domination of us by some power outside of this country. It is my recollection that the name came to be given to us by reason of one of the fathers of confederation recalling a biblical phrase with reference to God having dominion from sea to sea. That is how the term came into common use. As long as there is great loyalty and complete unity of the people, as long as we are working to make this country more widely known as the great country it is, I do not care whether we call it "Dominion of Canada" or "Canada". I do not wish to leave my seat and go out into the lobby when the vote comes. Would you be good enough to instruct me as to what I should do, Mr. Speaker, inasmuch as I do not think my opinion is worth registering one way or the other?

When the committee rose at six o'clock I was endeavouring to show how the railways, through their subsidies, were in a preferred position as compared with their competitors in the field of transportation. I want to refer to another instance in which the railways have preference over other types of transport, thus giving them a further advantage. In 1949 an order in council was passed, P.C. 8303, which altered the subsidy previously given to railways, steamships and trucks in the hauling of western feed grains and mill feeds to eastern Canada. By this order in council, P.C. 8303, a change was brought about in that subsidy whereby, if western feeds, western grains, and mill feeds were transported by rail they received a subsidy of $5.50; if hauled by water they received a subsidy of $4.15, but if hauled by truck the subsidy was withheld entirely. The evidence is clear in that case too that the railways, through government action, were given a very preferred position over that of trucks, and once again we find the government protecting their own railway business by government legislation.
Then, Mr. Chairman, we have the increase in freight rates granted to the railways just recently by the board of transport commissioners amounting to some 45 per cent, which

in effect increases the revenue of the railway. I am not saying whether that increase is justified or not, but it does undoubtedly put the railways in a preferred position.
On reviewing the evidence of the commission in regard to freight rates, the thing that struck me was that no endeavour was made to find out if there was an excess of overhead charges. It appears that any time the railways find themselves in difficulties, so far as revenue is concerned, all they have to do is to come to the government and apply for an increase in freight rates; and because one of the railways is government owned they have no trouble in getting all the increases they require. That is not true of the other competitors in this field of transportation.
As I indicated on another occasion, it was pointed out in the public accounts committee by one of the members of that committee that the over-all policy of the government was to give all their freight haulage to the railways or to water transport, and very little if any was to be given to trucks. That evidence seems to be borne out in all the things that I have indicated so far in my argument.
The railways are put in a preferred position by other government legislation. The house will remember that in 1938 legislation was passed which gave the railways the right to make agreed charges with business concerns which had freight to haul. That is, the railways could contract at a certain price to haul all or a portion of that company's freight, and thus the trucks were prevented from getting any of that business. Government legislation again gave the railways a very preferred position. I point out to you, Mr. Chairman, that several pieces of government legislation have discriminated against every other competitor of the railways so far as western Canada is concerned. This does not just merely happen; it is the policy of the government. There is no question about that, because they are the ones that are responsible for this legislation.
After the agreed charges were brought down, the judicial committee of the privy council recently decided that the effect of an agreed charge on the objecting carriers business and revenue is a relevant consideration for the transport board. The approval of an agreed charge has been withheld when it was shown to be unduly prejudicial to a water carrier who had participated in the carriage of a traffic and resulted in an undue or unfair advantage.
The Transport Act of 1938 gives to carriers by water and by air an opportunity to defend themselves but denies such an opportunity to carriers by motor vehicle.

There again, Mr. Chairman, we And that the board of transport commissioners very definitely make it impossible for motor transportation to take an appeal to that board no matter how unjust the action may be. It certainly goes without question that once again by legislation the government has placed facilities at the disposal of the railways and to the detriment of the only form of competitive transportation we have in western Canada, namely, the motor truck.
A while ago in regard to trucking I mentioned the national parks. I believe it was yesterday we talked about this matter when the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) assured me that when the trans-Canada highway was built through national parks the highway would be made available to trucks hauling through those parks, and not only through Banff but through Jasper, Yoho and the Kootenays.
Up to the present time through transportation by way of these parks has been absolutely forbidden. The Minister of Resources and Development pointed out that that was a regulation by the parks management themselves. However, when one understands that the national parks are under the control of the dominion government, then there can be no doubt about it that the order comes directly from this government.
There could be no more effective way of turning that entire transport business over to the railways than by barring trucks from passing through our national parks. That is exactly what was done in western Canada. All that business went to the railways. In effect it put a stop to all motor transport business between Alberta and British Columbia. Once again we find the government interfering with private enterprise in favour of its own government-owned railway.
It is contemplated that the trans-Canada highway may take seven years before it is completed. One must keep in mind that that is a long time for the railways to possess a further monopoly on those transportation facilities. As the trans-Canada highway is now being proceeded with the railways are becoming more concerned than ever about their competitors. They are not trying to compete, in the ordinary sense that one branch of free enterprise competes with another. They are not trying to reform their transportation business so as to bring it up to date. No; they are trying to drive out their competitors so that they will have the field completely to themselves.
As the legal representative of the province of Alberta stated before the royal commission, the day that motor transports are put off the road in favour of the railways, on that very
Supply-Transport
day we will see an increase in freight rates in western Canada. And, believe me, that is only too true.
What is the purpose of building the trans-Canada highway? The purpose is twofold; one is to convey tourists from one side of Canada to the other, and the other is to have a highway which will serve for truck transportation as well. The Minister of Resources and Development indicated the other day that that was the purpose for which this highway was being built. Of course, no sensible person would take issue with that. However, it would seem that the Department of Transport is not of that view. While I am speaking about the trans-Canada highway, and its relation to freight, may I read a portion of an editorial which appeared in the Western Producer of May 4, 1950. It has this to say:
Course of the highway across the west was never a very important issue, really. The big question was not where, but when the road would be built.
And then later:	.
It will be a strong link between the industrial east and the agricultural west and constitute a sound beachhead on the trade and geographic barrier separating the two. From the standpoint of national defence, the highway is imperative now that Canada is at the crossroads of world history.
The editorial points out that when this road is built it will constitute a sound beachhead on the trade and geographic barriers separating the east from the west. But if the railways had their way, certainly no such beachhead would be established; because it is only too well known that if it had not been for the railways trying to maintain a monopoly on the transportation of freight the trans-Canada highway would have been built years ago. I give the Minister of Resources and Development all the praise coming to him for pressing forward this work. It has been held too long in abeyance in order to help the privileged few.
Let us take note of the difference in the attitude taken by the United States government in the matter of highway traffic. It is true, as was pointed out this afternoon by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), that freight rates in the United States are higher than they are in Canada. But that country is certainly taking the opposite view so far as general transportation is concerned!, and in its attitude toward free enterprise, because not only are they encouraging truck transportation, but they are building express highways for the purpose of the greater and faster movement of freight by highways. The railways are forced to compete with those highways.
I say that if our railways cannot compete in rendering a service at as reasonable a rate

as is offered by motor transport, then they had better get out of the business because, if that is so, they are certainly becoming outmoded.
When the railways were presenting their evidence before the royal commission they made four general statements in regard to transportation. The first was that they wanted an amendment to the British North America Act to give to the federal government complete control over the highways. Now, what would be the purpose of the railways in wanting to turn over to the federal government the complete management of the highways? They know, without question, that that problem would be turned over to the board of transport commissioners and that then, as now, all the favours would go to the railways in order that they might maintain their complete monopoly.
May I ask the hon. member a question?

I would just as soon you
would wait. You will have another opportunity, and the time at my disposal is passing rapidly. In this connection I wish to quote from the Calgary Herald of December 15, 1949, to show that I am not the only one expressing this view. They say this in an editorial:
George A. Walker, chairman of the Canadian Pacific Railway, has suggested federal control of the highway trucking industry as one solution of the railways' difficulties. He has made this suggestion in the C.P.R.'s submission to the royal commission on transportation.
While we must accept the fact that the growth of truck competition is giving the railways cause for serious concern, we cannot agree with Mr. Walker that state regulation is the answer. It seems to us that a great number of other questions must be answered first.
It is customary for the railways to point out in this controversy-which, incidentally, has been going on for years-that while they move over permanent way which they have to maintain themselves at great expense, trucks move over highways which are built by the taxpayer. Therefore, they argue, trucks have a commanding competitive position.
But it seems to us that the question raised by this contention is not whether the state ought to regulate the trucking business, but whether trucks are paying their fair share of licence fees towards highway maintenance. So far as we know, very little serious research has been done into this problem.
If a heavy truck does more damage to highway surfaces in a year than is covered by its licence fee, then clearly that fee ought to be raised. There is no reason why trucks should be subsidized either by private motorists or by the general taxpayer.
May I interrupt there to say that they are not subsidized, but the railways are. The editorial continues:
But until it is established that trucks are being subsidized, it would be wrong to make any unsupported assumptions.

Now it is true that truck transport is often cheaper (and more convenient) than rail transport. Assuming that trucks pay their fair share of highway maintenance, this can only mean that for certain purposes truck transport is economically more efficient than rail transport.
And if this is so, there is no excuse whatever for regulating it into a position of lower efficiency- and that, whether we like it or not, would be the immediate effect of any control which forced trucks to charge as much as railways for carrying freight.
On some branch lines, and in some categories of freight, the railways apparently find it impossible to compete with trucks owing to their large fixed charges. There is no doubt that a healthy railway system is essential to the Canadian economy, but that cannot change the fact that where trucks can carry goods more cheaply and just as efficiently as railways, then trucks should get the business.
If, for strategic reasons, it is considered necessary to keep certain lines open despite the fact that they lose money in peacetime, then they should be maintained honestly and openly by direct subsidy as a charge against defence expenditures. But we do not see where further state control is going to help anybody.
May I endorse that statement as my own. I go on to the second submission by the railway which was: Eliminate highway services between railway points. That would have a terrible effect upon transportation particularly in western Canada. It would mean that trucks would not be able to operate between Calgary and Edmonton, between Edmonton and the Peace river, between Piegina and Saskatoon, between Toronto and Montreal or between Toronto and other points in Ontario. If that suggestion were followed it would mean that the railways would have a complete monopoly.	,
Then it is suggested that trucks should be restricted to hauls between 50 and 100 miles. When I was speaking the other day I indicated that that was the government's view as well and once again we see the Canadian Pacific carrying the ball for the government and the Canadian National.
The fourth submission was to eliminate highway subsidies by increasing user taxes. It seems to me that there the railway is getting into the realm of nazi dictatorship. What greater dictatorship would you want than evidence that they are trying to force their competitors out of business by increasing taxes on motor transport when at the same time they receive a government subsidy? The insinuation there is that trucks do not pay their way, but I should like to quote from an address by Mr. G. M. Parke, president of the Automotive Transport Association of Ontario Incorporated. The figures I intend to quote were taken from the statistics of the department of highways of Ontario so they must be correct. I quote:
Last year, commercial vehicles represented 18 per cent of the vehicles on our highways yet paid more than 50 per cent of the licence fees and in the neighbourhood of 40 per cent of the gas tax.

A study made two years ago revealed that the [DOT]owners of public commercial vehicles, although operating less than one per cent of the vehicles on our highways, paid approximately $6 million in licence fees and gas tax, or nearly 14 per cent of the total revenue collected by department of highways for 1947.
On the over-all picture of highway financing, department of highways statistics for the past ten years disclose receipts of $52 million in excess of the expenditure of $350,747,000. This expenditure not only included subsidies of some $77 million paid to counties, townships and towns and villages, as well as $4 million for roads in unincorporated townships and development roads under section IVB of the highway improvement act, but the complete cost of constructing and maintaining King's highways and development roads. A shining example is the construction of the Red lake road. The cost of $6,500,000 was paid out of current receipts.
That highway taxes in Ontario have been more than sufficient for the construction and maintenance of our fine highways is unquestionable. Suffice to say, commercial vehicle owners, paying close to 50 per cent of current highway costs, are more than paying their fair share.

Mr. Chairman, the question of freight rates is causing a great deal of comment. However today's discussion has not clarified the situation to a very great extent. It has provided an opportunity for our Conservative friends to move a vote of confidence in the government.
This rate problem seems to have originated with the history of this country, and it has certainly widespread ramifications throughout the whole economic structure of this nation.
The western provinces, at least this is what I understood from the remarks of the hon. member from Lake Centre, have complained of discrimination, unfairness and injustice. The Canadian National can hardly meet its
Supply-Transport
obligations on account of the tottering financial structure it has inherited from our successive governments and our political fancies. The Canadian Pacific, a private concern that makes every effort to provide the best service possible, can barely stand the competition of a government subsidized railway.
Our economic structure is therefore shaken and at times has difficulty in keeping its balance because of all the problems created by this situation.
This afternoon, the member for Regina City (Mr. McCusker) gave a short historical account of freight rates in western Canada. It seems they originated with the Crowsnest pass agreement, which goes back to 1897, I think, when certain maximum rates were set and guaranteed for the transport of grain and flour. Other conditions, for instance rates covering the transport of other commodities, were connected with this agreement.
As I see it, the agreement came about because western Canada had no choice in the matter of transport facilities, and was anxious to prevent the Canadian Pacific Railway from asking for a subsequent increase in its freight rates. On the other hand, those ceilings allowed the western provinces to ship a commodity vitally important to them. The rates set by the agreement have always been agreed to by the majority of the Canadian people, at the time of that decision as well as today.
This afternoon, the hon. member for Lake Centre championed the cause of all those who favour the maximum rates set in the agreement. I wish to remind him that around 1918 the Conservative party wanted to put aside that agreement and substitute therefor the authority of the board of transport commissioners. He seemed to have a good memory this afternoon. However, I would like to put on the record a brief account of what happened between 1922 and 1925 in connection with this problem. The following excerpt is taken from page 189 of the report of the royal commission on dominion-provincial relations, volume II-that is the Rowell-Sirois commission. I quote:
Between those who thought the Crowsnest Pass Agreement Act (which antedated the bill creating the board of railway commissioners by six years) should be repealed, leaving freight rates in the west to be fixed by the railways subject to appeals to the board, and those who held that these rates should be continued as a protection to an area which was not favoured with water competition, a conflict began in 1922 which was fought out in special parliamentary committees, in cases before the board of railway commissioners, in references to the supreme court, in appeals to the governor in council and in parliament itself. In the result,

Supply-Transport
the principle that it was proper for parliament to put statutory limits to the powers of the railway commission was clearly established by the retention in the order in council of June 5, 1925, of the grain and flour provisions of the Crowsnest pass agreement.
Today, the Conservative party requests the abolition of the commission and poses as the great champion of the agreement that owes its survival to the Liberal party.
Naturally, in view of his party's previous position, I am only mildly interested in the invitation of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) to support his amendment.
It will be seen, therefore, that since 1925 freight rates for grain and flour have remained the same and recent increases could not be brought into effect.
We are faced here with an important question. Whenever a preferential rate is provided for certain goods in the lower classes, should not freight rates on goods in the higher classes compensate for the loss sustained in the first case? I merely want to point out the matter now and will refer to it again in a moment.
At the other end of the country, that is to say, in the maritimes, new rates have been brought into effect under the Maritime Freight Rates Act.
The central provinces, that is Quebec and Ontario, seeing these means of transportation grow with amazing rapidity, were, in turn, faced with a problem, since competition began to appear between the various forms of transportation.
It was then that the C.N.R. and the C.P.R. were forced to revise their rates in order to meet this competition. Certain adjustments had to be made, which caused the maritimes to lose the advantage that the 20 per cent reduction had originally brought them.
There obtained then, in some regions, conditions which were bound to affect the economic stability of a group of provinces, endangered by the competition which had arisen in the central provinces, which were bound by an agreement with another part of the country where a maximum price was imposed because of the greater volume of transportable goods. It was therefore not easy to find a formula satisfactory to Canadians of all regions, without imposing too heavy a burden on the provinces of Ontario and Quebec in order to maintain the railway system which Canada now enjoys.
As I said at the beginning of my remarks, if there is a special rate for a certain class

of commodities, it is only normal that another class of commodities should compensate for the loss incurred. Otherwise, the government would be forced to subsidize the railways in order to compensate for the loss in revenue they would necessarily sustain. Then, who is going to assume these responsibilities? I have often heard that Quebec and Ontario are paying their substantial share.
I am asked if I have anything to suggest. Yes, I have something to suggest, though it is something which does not agree with the suggestion made by the leader of the opposition. As a matter of fact, the board of transport commissioners, with all its experience, is in my estimation the organization which is most likely to bring about the best solution. Perhaps, it might be advisable that it should undergo certain changes, but it is out of the question that it should be dispensed with completely.
It seems that, as the years go by, the tendency is to equalize the freight rates in so far as certain higher grades of commodities are concerned. It seems also that there is now a tendency to grant special rates on primary products when the particular economy of a district is affected. If it is the decision of this government to relieve the situation by way of grants, why not add them to the maximum prices of these products? We would thus be killing two birds with one stone, helping at the same time the economy of the district concerned and that of our railways.
I have not carefully considered the various reasons put forth in favour of the horizontal increase in rates but, to my mind, it stems from the financial position of the railways.
The plight of the Canadian National, whose financial structure is heavily burdened by all sorts of commitments and in some cases crippled by extravagance, is daily growing worse. The Canadian Pacific, a private company, has to compete with a government enterprise and does not earn enough revenue to meet this competition.
Naturally, I am against any increase in freight rates but I have reason to believe that it is safer and wiser to await the findings of the royal commission before overthrowing, by a single vote, what generations have tried to build, in the past few decades, in the field of transportation.
I will not mention the C.C.F. amendment. It is, in effect, a motion of non-confidence in

the government and I am not ready to accept their nationalization program that borders, if followed to its logical conclusion, on another doctrine which is not to my liking either.

Mr. Chairman, we have had a long discussion on freight rates today, and I do not intend to take much of the time of the committee. It is not my intention to discuss the merits or demerits of the amendment or the amendment to the amendment. Member after member has already discussed the incompetence of the board of transport commissioners. I will only say that if they are half as incompetent as the leader of the opposition and the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar have accused them of being there is no reason why they should not go. I have heard railway rates discussed on many occasions in this chamber, and I took part when we were discussing the 21 per cent increase in freight rates in 1948. When it was instituted we of the maritime provinces did not oppose the increase as such, because we realized that railway rates had to be raised. What we did oppose was the method of the increase, and what we considered and believed was unjust discrimination against the maritime provinces. We felt then as we feel now, that increases in railway freight rates should be borne equally by all sections of the country and not as it is today.
There has been a 45 per cent increase since 1946. We believe that the horizontal method [DOT]-and I think anyone who studies it will come to the same conclusion-discriminates against the people of the three maritime provinces as it does against the people of western Canada. It is something that should be corrected. I do not think the board of transport commissioners has been considering the matter of railway freight rates from the the broad point of view that it should take, but rather from what might be termed a dollar and cents point of view. I think railway rates should be considered from the point of view of the development of trade in all sections of the country, the geographical position in which different sections of the country find themselves, and more particularly, as I think was the case in the early days, in the spirit of confederation.
Railways and railway freight rates have been a most important consideration for the people of the maritime provinces from the days when this country first became the Dominion of Canada. As a matter of fact the economic existence of the three maritime provinces depended to a great extent on the railways and on cheap freight rates. One of
Supply-Transport
the main conditions under which the maritime provinces came into confederation was that we would be given satisfactory railway transportation, and that we would also be given satisfactory freight rates. To indicate just how the present rates are considered in my own province I should like to read an article which appeared in the Saint John Telegraph-Journal of March 2, and which I think expresses it far better than I could:
Another Freight Rate Blow
The latest horizontal increase in railway freight rates, authorized yesterday by the board of transport commissioners, is another blow at the economy of this part of Canada. It will make it more difficult for New Brunswickers to do business, will aggravate the unemployment problem, and will tend to advance the cost of living.
The high cost of transportation has always been a burden on this region and a factor calculated to retard industrial development. And whenever the freight rates are advanced on a flat percentage basis the position of this province becomes worse.
That is the way they are being advanced at the present time.
That's because we are far from the country's largest markets and its main sources of raw materials, and are up against long rail hauls.
Percentage increases obviously bear more heavily on long haul than on short haul shippers. Then, too, in central Canada rail rates are held down to meet truck and water competition. In New Brunswick the railways do not face such competition nearly as much, and are thus not compelled to reduce rates to hold the traffic . . .
In hearing the railway applications for higher rates, the board of transport commissioners contended that it could not consider the economic implications from the standpoint of the various regions. It held that this was not within its jurisdiction.
That is what I said a few moments ago, that this matter was considered from the dollar and cents point of view and not from the broad point of view, as I think it should have been.
The royal commission on transportation, set up by the federal government to consider all phases of the freight rate issue, has wider powers. Our best hope now seems to be that this tribunal will find a more equitable way of distributing the freight rate burden, so that while the railways will get the revenue they need, undue hardship will not be imposed on all provinces but Ontario and Quebec. Certainly, horizontal rate increases are wrong in principle, and not in the best interests of Canada.
As I said a short time' ago, Mr. Chairman, since the days of confederation we have realized that railways were one of our chief considerations. I shall not weary hon. members this evening with the history of the railway situation in the maritime provinces from the time of confederation, but I should like to mention just a few points. From 1867 to 1912 the maritime provinces were fairly well treated as far as freight rates were concerned. We in those provinces were left

Supply-Transport
more or less to adjust our own freight rates. In 1912, however, when the Intercolonial railway was taken over, the first increase in rates was brought about. That increase amounted to 10 per cent, and I point out to hon. gentlemen that it applied in the maritime provinces only. In 1915 there was a 5 per cent increase, again only in the maritime provinces. Then in 1918 there was a 15 per cent increase, so the increases amounted to 30 per cent in a little over six years. The last increase, of course, applied to all Canada. These increases placed such an intolerable burden upon the economy of the maritime provinces that something had to be done. The condition was such that in 1925 members of parliament from the maritime provinces, Conservative and Liberal alike, joined in protest and presented to this house what was then called their claim for maritime rights. If I may say so, Mr. Chairman, I believe the action of the maritime province members in joining together in 1925 to urge what they felt were the rights of their provinces should set an example to the maritime province members of today. I hope all members from the maritimes will unite at this time to see if they cannot get our rights adjusted in this matter of rates.
The result of the agitation for maritime rights was the appointment in 1926 of what was known as the Duncan commission. Sir Andrew Rae Duncan as chairman made a survey of conditions in the maritime provinces and his 'commission made many recommendations, some of which have been implemented while others have not. I do not intend to go into those questions this evening, but as far as our railways were concerned it was recommended that this matter should be very carefully considered, and as a result a 20 per cent reduction on rail rates within the maritime provinces was brought about. The opinion is sometimes expressed in this house that this 20 per cent reduction in rail rates was given the maritime provinces because of the long rail haul, but that is not entirely true. After investigation, it was found that taking 100 as the index of operation at that time, the figure for the maritime provinces was 192 while the figure for the other parts of Canada was 155. So the 20 per cent reduction was not because of the long rail haul but because of this situation which had grown up over a period of years. It was also given us in order to encourage industry. We had lost much of our industry in the maritime provinces, and it was felt that if we were to compete with industry in other parts of Canada we must have some encouragement.
I was rather surprised to learn that there is some misunderstanding in New Brunswick

in reference to this 20 per cent reduction, and particularly as to the submission that has been made to the royal commission on transportation. I understand the government of New Brunswick has recommended that the 20 per cent reduction under the Maritime Freight Rates Act, which now applies only to transportation within the provinces and west out of the provinces, should apply also to freight coming east into the maritimes. I have not sufficient information to say whether this should or should not be done; I believe there are strong arguments on each side. It does seem to me, however, a sad commentary on the situation in our province that the government should feel that the days of industry and manufacturing in New Brunswick must be almost over. Now we can say to the manufacturers in other parts of Canada, "You shall have this 20 per cent increase on freight coming into our province because it looks as though the freight structure we have will mean there will be no more manufacturing in our province". It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that must be the attitude which some of the people, and the government of our province, are taking at the present time. The hon. member for Cape Breton South spoke about the protection of our industries. He said that we only had a few industries in New Brunswick, and that may be true. He said that it did not make much difference, or words to that effect, whether or not those industries were saved. We know that the member for Cape Breton South is not in favour of private enterprise, and probably his remarks were coloured somewhat by that view.
I know personally that we have splendid industries in the maritime provinces. Over a period of years they have established a reputation for the excellence of their quality, and it is for that reason they are continuing. I could mention our boot and shoe industry in Fredericton; the enterprise foundry in Sackville; our chocolate industry, in both Halifax and St. Stephen; the Fawcett factory in Sackville; the Simms Brush Company in Saint John, and Stanfield underwear in Truro and others of the same quality and standing. Our industries have built a reputation for quality, Mr. Chairman, and it is for that reason more than any other that they have survived. It is not my intention to labour that point, but I do think it worth bringing to the attention of this house, that in the past the maritime provinces had a 20 per cent protection which built up our industries. With the loss of so many industries, with the high freight rates we now have, and the hopelessness which you will find if this situation continues-it will be difficult to

encourage new industry or retain the old. The only hope we shall have will be from our basic industries.
I feel that the maritime provinces are back to the position in which they were in 1926 when the Duncan commission reported on the maritime claim. I should like to read what the Duncan commission said about our claims in its report to the federal government:
The Intercolonial railway was completed in 1876, and it w.ould appear from the evidence we have received that from then until 1912 the interests of the maritime provinces were fairly well safeguarded.
I mentioned that a few moments ago.
The lower level of rates that prevailed on the Intercolonial railway system prior to 1912, is, in our view, rightly to be interpreted as the fulfilment by successive governments of the policy and pledges that surrounded the railway from its inception . . .
As I pointed out, the Duncan commission found that these confederation pledges had been followed. We had hoped that the injustice which had been done would be corrected. It was corrected, as I say, by the Maritime Freight Rates Act. Today the situation is as bad as ever. The Maritime Freight Rates Act came into force in 1928, just prior to the depression. We did hope there would be more industry attracted to the maritime provinces, and the province of New Brunswick, but as you know during the depression years very little industry was attracted to any part of Canada. The war followed the depression; and, so far as the Maritime Freight Rates Act is concerned, it really has not had an opportunity of operating in the maritime provinces to encourage industry.
I feel that the whole freight rate situation needs a complete overhaul. The disadvantages from a geographical point of view and other factors should receive every consideration. Every increase in the railway rates has meant less business in our province. We are in a different position today from what we were a number of years ago. Our overseas markets are lost. We do not sell our apples, for instance, in Great Britain as we did a few years ago. The apple producers have to turn to Toronto and Montreal, as well as the other parts of Canada, in order to sell their products. This means that the higher freight rates put another burden on the apple producers of the Annapolis valley and the Saint John valley. The same considerations apply, Mr. Chairman, to our lumber, our potatoes, our fish and other primary products.
The other day I noticed in one of the papers an article with which I quite agreed, to the effect we have too many miles of railway in Canada. By that I do not mean that in new territory, such as mining territory in the north country, where there are great natural

resources, we should not have new lines of railway. In the various provinces, however, there are old branch lines which are not necessary. Trucks are carrying most of the freight, and buses are carrying most of the passengers. I hope this transportation commission will give careful study to the matter, and recommend the elimination of many of these lines which are today only a burden on the country.
The hon. member for Bow River spoke of truck transportation. This is a matter, of course, which will have to be given careful consideration. I believe there is a place for the trucks in our transportation system, just as there is a place for our railways, our air transports, and our water transports. I believe this is something to which the royal commission should give careful study. I do not believe our transportation problems are such that they cannot be solved. I feel they can be solved in the best interests of all the people of Canada, and in a way that will make no section of Canada suffer. So far as this royal commission is concerned, I note that they are preparing their report and I do hope it will be a satisfactory one. I have great faith in that commission. The chairman of the commission, the Hon. Mr. Turgeon, is from my own province of New Brunswick. Perhaps that is one reason why I have faith in it. I have great faith that this problem of transportation will be solved, and that all sections of the Dominion of Canada will be properly served. No one could contemplate for one moment the loss of our railways. Canada would not be a nation long if that should happen. In my opinion the competition with which the railways have to contend must be controlled.
It is not my intention to speak any longer tonight. As I said a few moments ago, I do hope that justice will be done to all sections of Canada, whether it be in the matter of transportation, economic production or industry; that we will be protected and that every section will have the same opportunity for progress and prosperity.

That sort of thinking goes hand in glove with the thinking of the Conservative party across this country over a long, long period of time.
I say that because that is exactly what took place in 1903. In 1903 it was the responsibility of the governor in council and of the privy council to deal with matters affecting freight rates. In fact there was a subcommittee of the cabinet whose responsibility it was to fix rates. At that time, because of the difficulty of such a committee in dealing with matters of this kind, the government appointed Professor McLean, who had had a great deal of experience in matters concerning freight rates, and who had spent all his life studying the question.
After having made an investigation and having reported to the government, he gave the reason why the railway committee of the privy council was unable to do an efficient and effective job with reference to freight rates. I quote:
The committee has been unable, owing to its organization, to grapple effectively with the problem presented. It has been impossible, owing to its stationary character, to deal effectively with questions pertaining to rates and preferences. A more migratory body could deal more effectively with these matters.
The defects of the railway committee as a regulator of railway transportation I would place under the following heads:
1.	It has a dual function, political and administrative.
2.	The lack of migratory organization renders it impossible to deal effectively with complaints.
3.	The distances to be travelled by complainants render the expense too great.
4.	There is lack of technical training for the work.
5.	The existing organization is not sufficiently permanent.
In my opinion, the only way to put the matter of railway regulation on a more satisfactory footing in Canada is by entrusting it to a railway commission composed of men of technical training, who

And that is why I say that their thinking is at least forty-five years old.
It never should be the responsibility of the governor in council to fix freight rates. It never should be the responsibility of the governor in council to determine the freight rate structure.

I am coming to that. True, it has a responsibility under section 52 which is judicial in nature. That it should exercise powers of a judicial nature?-yes. It has done that by way of hearing petitions by provinces. It will do it again with reference to petitions now before it. But that the governor in council should do those very things which were recommended against by Professor McLean would be, I say, a retrograde step, and one which I am sure the government would never think of taking.

But these increases, the 20 per cent case and the 30 per cent case, do not apply to grain rates and were never intended to apply to them.

But they apply to the
machines and materials that enter into the cost of production. That is what I meant.

But that is not what the hon. member said. I say to the hon. member that freight rates on grain and grain products have not been increased since 1897 except as already stated. As a matter of fact those two decisions exempt grain products, whether going to the east by way of Fort William and Armstrong or to the west by way of Vancouver and Prince Rupert; and the hon. gentleman well knows the position in reference to the Crowsnest rate.
There are other matters with which I would like to deal, but let me summarize the position in this way. The amendment of the leader of the opposition will accomplish nothing. It does not begin to meet the problem. I submit that the problem can only be met, first toy the investigation being conducted by the board of transport commissioners with the object of

Supply-Transport
equalizing rates where there is unjust discrimination, and second, by the findings of the royal commission. I think the committee should be reminded that discrimination exists in many parts of Canada. I do not think that can be denied; it has always been the case. It is unfair or unjust discrimination with which the board seeks to deal. The other method adopted by the government to meet this problem was the appointment of a royal commission on transportation to which terms of reference were assigned so that it might report and advise the government on these matters. Meanwhile the provinces have filed a petition. The government will hear that petition and give it the same careful consideration that was given an earlier petition.
I have not given any thought to the question of whether or not the subamendment is in order, but I submit that neither the amendment nor the subamendment, nor both together, could begin to solve the problem. This difficulty will not be overcome by moving an amendment of that sort and putting the board of transport commissioners out of existence. Of all the groups or organizations in Canada that might deal with the freight rate structure of our country, I believe the board of transport commissioners is the one to do it, because that board has the experience and knowledge. It has been said they have not the staff, but that is not so; they have the staff. In the first place they have a traffic department composed of some twenty experts. They have a bureau of transportation economics composed of some forty men, and in all they have some 130 people who are familiar with this whole subject.
I consider this amendment and the subamendment in the nature of a vote of want of confidence; and even if they were to carry- I know they will not, but if perchance they should-we would not have a solution to the problem. I say the only way to meet the difficulties facing us at the moment is the manner adopted by the government, first by directing the board to equalize the rate structure, and second by setting up the royal commission to advise the government on matters of policy. The attitude adopted by hon. gentlemen opposite is both critical and destructive, and would not begin to meet the problem in any way.
Mr. Chairman, I would not-
Anticlimax.
The anticlimax came when the vote was taken on the motion of the hon. member.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Peace River tried to get the floor even before the hon. member for Bow River spoke this afternoon. Therefore in all fairness I think I should recognize him now.

Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman. Certainly I do not wish to keep the hon. member for Cariboo from expressing his opinion on this matter. As a matter of fact I think every hon. member of this house should recognize the importance of this problem and have something to say about it.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the minister who just finished speaking began his address this evening in rather moderate tones. He proceeded to characterize the various speeches that had been made up to that time when he introduced his rebuttal. He classified them in this way; the boldest speech was made by the leader of the opposition; the mildest speech by the leader of the C.C.F. and his colleague from Cape Breton South; the most indignant speech by the member for Lake Centre; and the loudest speech by the member for Lethbridge. It is always wise for people who begin to classify contributions of others to take a little care with their own. Frankly, I would classify the minister's speech as the loudest of the day, the most excited, the most strident, the most raucous, and the most evasive. As a matter of fact, I was surprised that he allowed himself to be carried away by the sound of his own voice. At various stages of his address, he reminded me a great deal of a minister who had to yell like hell when his argument was weak.
I would not speak in this debate, Mr. Chairman, if I did not have a different approach from those who have spoken thus far. In the course of the case which I shall present I do not . intend to vilify anybody, to castigate the board of transport commissioners, or set myself up as the arbiter of the freight rate structure of this country. I do have a suggestion to make, and I hope it will be received in the spirit in which it is given. It is a constructive approach, and something that has not yet been brought to the attention of this house.
Before I launch into it, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say that during the course of the minister's address he said that no evidence since a certain date, I think it was 1925 or 1923, had been brought to show where discrimination lies. I believe he was speaking of the statement made by the member for Lake Centre that there was discrimination in Canada. It depends, of course, on how you

define discrimination. I am all too aware of the way that the board of transport commissioners, and of course the Minister of Transport, define discrimination. They take the position that there is no discrimination unless some individual considers himself to be aggrieved, or unless the railways charge someone in a certain region a rate that is different from that which they would charge some other person in the same region for the same haul.
Will the hon. member allow an interruption?
Yes.
I merely wanted to say that the Railway Act defines discrimination, and the board is bound by what is set out in the act.

That is very good, and it falls
right in with the case I want to present. There is discrimination as between region and region in this country, and the minister knows that such discrimination exists. Furthermore, he knows that the examples that were produced today by my colleague the member for Lethbridge were bona fide examples of discrimination as between region and region. I know full well that when the minister says the board of transport commissioners is not charged with the responsibility, at the moment, of removing regional discrimination, he speaks the truth. He says that all the board can do is to remove unjust discrimination, and that is true. The complaint we have, Mr. Chairman, is that the board of transport commissioners have not been given
Supply-Transport
a directive from this government to remove regional discrimination, as well as unjust discrimination between persons within a region. It is that case I want to present when I start in earnest with my presentation.
It is so near eleven o'clock, Mr. Chairman, that I would not like to launch into the argument I wish to present, and then break it off in a minute or two. I wish you would allow me to adjourn the debate.
Item stands.
Progress reported.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on
Monday at eleven o'clock we shall take up the following small bills: Bill No. 252, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935; Bill No. 263, to amend the Electricity Inspection Act, 1928; Bill No. 264, to amend the Gas Inspection Act; and perhaps Bill No. 135, if time is left.
At three o'clock we shall ask to revert to motions, and the Secretary of State for External Affairs will make a statement on the conference held in London by the ministers of the nations signatory to the Atlantic pact. We shall then move to go into supply, and I understand there will be a discussion of external affairs. When this motion is carried, we shall call one item of the secretary of state to stand, and we shall proceed with the estimates of veterans affairs.
At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
